items.name: Slow Zoom In
items.prompt: Slow optical zoom in on [Subject], camera body locked on a heavy tripod, lens gradually tightening over several seconds, background compression increasing, no physical dolly, prestige-drama patience. For motion: the lens slowly zooms in for 6 seconds while the camera body stays locked and the subject stays centered.
items.definition: A slow zoom in is slow zoom in cinematography that tightens the frame by increasing focal length while the camera body stays locked. Perspective relations stay fixed: the world does not slide, it only enlarges as the lens compresses space.

items.name: Slow Zoom Out
items.prompt: Slow optical zoom out from [Subject], tripod locked, the frame breathing open to reveal surrounding architecture and negative space, no camera body travel. For motion: the lens slowly zooms out for 6 seconds from a tight frame on [Subject] into a wider environment.
items.definition: A slow zoom out widens the frame by decreasing focal length while the support stays put. More architecture and negative space enter the picture, yet the camera never travels, so true parallax does not appear.

items.name: Crash Zoom In
items.prompt: Aggressive crash zoom into [Subject], snap optical punch-in under one second, radial motion blur, Shaw Brothers energy, then a hard hold on the tight frame. For motion: sudden crash zoom into [Subject] in under a second, then hold.
items.definition: A crash zoom is a rapid focal-length snap from a wider frame into a detail, usually without moving the camera. The punch is optical and conspicuous: size changes faster than a body can walk.

items.name: Crash Zoom Out
items.prompt: Sudden crash zoom out from [Subject], the environment exploding into view in a fraction of a second, then a locked wide hold. For motion: snap zoom out from [Subject] in under a second, revealing the wider scene, then hold.
items.definition: A crash zoom out is a sudden, fast widening of the lens from a tight frame into a much wider one, usually without moving the camera. It dumps the subject back into the environment in a fraction of a second.

items.name: Dolly In
items.prompt: Physical dolly in toward [Subject] on track, camera body gliding forward, parallax shifting foreground against background, 40mm spherical, buttery traction. For motion: the camera physically dollies forward toward [Subject] for 6 seconds.
items.definition: A dolly in shot moves the entire camera through space on a wheeled or tracked support, advancing toward the subject at a measured pace. The nodal point walks, so foreground and background shift in parallax as the surroundings are progressively excluded.

items.name: Dolly Out
items.prompt: Physical dolly out from [Subject], camera retreating on track, the world widening with true parallax, subject shrinking inside architecture. For motion: the camera physically dollies backward away from [Subject], revealing more environment with parallax.
items.definition: A dolly out shot withdraws the entire camera through space on a wheeled or tracked support. The world widens with true parallax, and the subject shrinks inside architecture because the station point has actually retreated.

items.name: Dolly Left
items.prompt: Lateral dolly left across [Subject], camera sliding sideways on track, background planes peeling in parallax, subject tracked in frame. For motion: the camera slides left on a dolly, keeping [Subject] in frame, background parallax visible.
items.definition: A dolly left, also called a truck left, slides the whole camera sideways to the left on wheels or track. The lens stays aimed with the subject while background planes peel past in parallax.

items.name: Dolly Right
items.prompt: Lateral dolly right across [Subject], smooth sideways travel, layered parallax, locked horizon. For motion: the camera slides right on a dolly, keeping [Subject] framed, smooth lateral parallax.
items.definition: A dolly right, or truck right, moves the camera body sideways to the right without panning. New space enters from one side of the frame while the other side exits, and layered parallax proves the translation.

items.name: Pan Left
items.prompt: Slow pan left from a locked tripod across [Subject], camera rotating on its vertical axis, horizon level, revealing new architecture to the left. For motion: the camera pans left from a fixed tripod, sweeping across [Subject] and the environment.
items.definition: A pan left is pan shot cinematography that rotates the camera on a fixed tripod or head around its vertical axis, sweeping the view to the left. The support does not travel; only the direction of the lens changes.

items.name: Pan Right
items.prompt: Slow pan right from a locked tripod across [Subject], fluid head rotation, level horizon, a continuous horizontal reveal. For motion: the camera pans right from a fixed tripod across [Subject].
items.definition: A pan right shot is a horizontal rotation of a locked-off camera toward the right. It connects two parts of the same geography in one continuous turn from a single station point.

items.name: Tilt Up
items.prompt: Slow tilt up from [Subject], camera rotating on its horizontal axis, climbing from ground detail to face or from face to towering architecture. For motion: the camera tilts up from a fixed position, starting low on [Subject] and climbing vertically.
items.definition: A tilt up shot rotates the camera vertically around a fixed position, climbing from a lower composition to a higher one. The tripod does not rise; only pitch changes, so the viewpoint height stays the same.

items.name: Tilt Down
items.prompt: Slow tilt down onto [Subject], starting in sky or ceiling and descending to the figure, a measured vertical scan. For motion: the camera tilts down from above onto [Subject], revealing the figure from head to environment.
items.definition: A tilt-down rotates the camera vertically from a fixed position, starting higher and ending lower. It can drop from sky or architecture onto a person or object without moving the tripod.

items.name: Whip Pan
items.prompt: Violent whip pan off [Subject], horizontal motion blur streaking the world into ribbons, then a snap resolve on the next beat. For motion: extremely fast whip pan away from [Subject], heavy horizontal motion blur, then a sharp stop.
items.definition: A whip pan pans so quickly that the image blurs into horizontal streaks, then snaps to a new composition. Two shots can be joined inside compatible directional motion blur, creating the impression of one fast reorientation.

items.name: Whip Tilt
items.prompt: Violent vertical whip tilt across [Subject], the frame ripping up or down with motion blur, then a hard stop. For motion: extremely fast vertical whip tilt across [Subject] with motion blur, then a hard stop.
items.definition: A whip tilt is a violent, motion-blurred vertical rotation of the camera, then a hard stop. It is the up-or-down cousin of a whip pan: shock through speed, not through traveling the support.

items.name: Pedestal Up
items.prompt: Pedestal up on [Subject], camera rising vertically on a column with no tilt change, eyeline climbing, architecture sliding down the frame. For motion: the camera rises straight up on a pedestal, keeping the same tilt, lifting past [Subject].
items.definition: A pedestal shot moves the entire camera vertically without changing its tilt. The lens rises on a column, eyeline climbs, and architecture slides down the frame while pitch stays constant.

items.name: Pedestal Down
items.prompt: Pedestal down on [Subject], camera lowering vertically, no tilt, a calm descent through the same axis. For motion: the camera lowers straight down on a pedestal, keeping tilt constant, settling onto [Subject].
items.definition: A pedestal down lowers the entire camera vertically without changing its tilt. The descent stays on one axis: a calm drop through the same look, not a nod and not a crane swoop.

items.name: Crane Up
items.prompt: Majestic crane up from [Subject], camera rising and easing backward on a Technocrane, the individual becoming one figure inside a vast environment, golden or blue-hour air, 35mm Signature Prime. For motion: the camera cranes smoothly upward and slightly backward from shoulder height, rising above [Subject] to reveal the true surrounding scale.
items.definition: A crane shot lifts the camera on a jib or Technocrane, often easing backward at the same time, so the frame climbs from a human scale into a wider view of the location. Height change is the point, and a little boom-out keeps the subject from sliding off the bottom of the frame.

items.name: Crane Down
items.prompt: Crane down onto [Subject], starting high and descending into a human-scale frame, the world collapsing from map to face. For motion: the camera cranes down from a high wide view into a closer frame on [Subject].
items.definition: A crane down shot lowers the camera on an arm from a high wide view into a human-scale frame. The world collapses from map to face because the lens occupies new heights, not because it merely nods.

items.name: Crane Over
items.prompt: Crane over [Subject], the arm rising and arcing forward until the camera looks nearly straight down, a continuous climb into overhead. For motion: the camera cranes up and over [Subject], finishing in a high downward angle.
items.definition: A crane-over lifts and arcs the camera on a jib or crane until it looks down on the scene from above. Height and angle change together in one move, turning the floor into a map.

items.name: Jib Shot
items.prompt: Short jib move on [Subject], a compact crane arm lifting or sweeping a few feet, more intimate than a full Technocrane, elegant vertical accent. For motion: a compact jib arm lifts a few feet above [Subject] with a gentle sweep.
items.definition: A jib shot uses a short pivoting arm to raise, lower, or sweep the camera a few feet. It is a compact crane: small height change, often over a table, a walk, or a two-shot.

items.name: 360-Degree Orbit
items.prompt: Full 360-degree orbit around [Subject], camera circling at constant radius, background becoming a continuous ribbon of light, centripetal romantic or predatory energy. For motion: the camera orbits 360 degrees around [Subject], always facing them, background wrapping as a ribbon of light.
items.definition: A 360-degree orbit shot circles the subject through a full turn, usually at a constant radius, always facing them. The background becomes a continuous ribbon while the person stays the center of interest.

items.name: Arc Left
items.prompt: 90-degree arc left around [Subject], curved dolly, always facing the figure, background sliding, a quarter-orbit instead of a full spin. For motion: the camera arcs left about 90 degrees around [Subject], always facing them.
items.definition: An arc left is a curved dolly that travels partway around the subject while staying aimed at them. The camera's axis on the conversation or room changes without a cut, usually about a quarter-orbit.

items.name: Arc Right
items.prompt: 90-degree arc right around [Subject], curved travel, continuous eyeline on the figure. For motion: the camera arcs right about 90 degrees around [Subject], always facing them.
items.definition: An arc right is a partial orbit to the right, usually about a quarter turn, with the lens remaining on the subject. Background slides while eyeline and distance stay roughly constant.

items.name: Tracking Shot
items.prompt: Lateral tracking shot of [Subject], camera matching pace on a parallel path, shoulder height, parallax of foreground, mid-ground, and deep background. For motion: the camera tracks alongside [Subject] at walking pace, holding a consistent distance.
items.definition: A tracking shot moves with, beside, ahead of, or behind a moving subject, typically matching pace on a parallel path. The person supplies the motion; the camera keeps distance, height, and scale while foreground, mid-ground, and deep background peel.

items.name: Follow Shot
items.prompt: Follow shot behind [Subject], camera trailing at a fixed offset, the back of the head as foreground, the world opening ahead. For motion: the camera follows behind [Subject], matching their movement through the space.
items.definition: A follow shot trails a moving subject at a fixed offset, usually from behind. The back of the head becomes foreground and the world opens ahead, so pursuit, haunting, or arrival is felt as walking into space.

items.name: Steadicam
items.prompt: Steadicam floating with [Subject] through connected spaces, preternatural smoothness, operator walking, light temperatures shifting as rooms change. For motion: smooth Steadicam move floating with [Subject] through the environment, no footfall shake.
items.definition: Steadicam is a mechanical stabilizing system using a sled, arm, and vest, so an operator can walk while the camera floats. The path can connect rooms with a smoothness that is neither handheld tremor nor dolly traction.

items.name: Handheld
items.prompt: Handheld camera on [Subject], breathing micro-shake, documentary immediacy, Super 16 grain feel, the operator's body in the frame's nerves. For motion: handheld camera with natural operator shake holding [Subject] in frame.
items.definition: A handheld camera is operated from the body without a stabilizing vest or gimbal, so breathing, micro-shake, and mass stay in the frame. The image has the nerves of a person holding weight, not a track and not a motor.

items.name: Gimbal Shot
items.prompt: Gimbal move with [Subject], electronically stabilized but still human-carried, smoother than handheld, freer than dolly, modern action grammar. For motion: smooth gimbal move following [Subject], stabilized but slightly human, gliding through the space.
items.definition: A gimbal shot uses motorized stabilization for smooth handheld or vehicle-mounted movement. Electronic inertia damps roll and high-frequency shake while a human still carries the camera, freer than a dolly and cleaner than raw handheld.

items.name: FPV Drone
items.prompt: FPV drone racing past [Subject], first-person flight, banking turns, proximity to architecture, motion blur on edges, extreme sports camera path. For motion: FPV drone flies past and around [Subject] with banking turns and proximity to structures.
items.definition: An FPV drone shot is first-person aerial flying: the camera banks, dives, and threads architecture at high speed. It is proximity and flight, a racing craft with a lens, not a slow crane and not a high establishing hover.

items.name: Aerial Pullback
items.prompt: Aerial pullback from [Subject], camera rising and receding until the figure is a speck in geography, helicopter or high drone grammar, landscape taking the frame. For motion: the camera rises and pulls back from [Subject] until the surrounding landscape dominates.
items.definition: An aerial pullback rises and recedes until a person or building becomes a small mark in a landscape. The move hands the scene from a character to geography, from helicopter or high-drone height rather than from a ground crane.

items.name: Aerial Push In
items.prompt: Aerial push in toward [Subject] from high altitude, descending and tightening from map to person, a high view finding a face. For motion: the camera descends and pushes in from a high aerial toward [Subject].
items.definition: An aerial push in starts high and descends or tightens until a single figure reads in the map. It picks one human out of a city, crowd, or terrain from altitude.

items.name: Push In
items.prompt: Imperceptibly slow push in on [Subject], the camera closing from medium to medium close-up so gradually the audience feels walls closing before they notice motion. For motion: very slow push in toward [Subject] over 6 seconds, medium into medium close-up.
items.definition: A push in shot moves physically or virtually closer to the subject so size grows because the camera walks. It is a short pressure advance, often so gradual the audience feels the walls close before they notice motion.

items.name: Pull Out
items.prompt: Slow pull out from [Subject], intimacy widening into environment, the person remaining while the world claims them. For motion: slow pull out from [Subject], the frame widening to reveal the environment.
items.definition: A pull out shot moves physically or virtually away from the subject so more environment enters around a person or detail. Intimacy widens into context without changing lenses.

items.name: Static Locked-Off
items.prompt: Perfectly static locked-off shot of [Subject], heavy tripod, zero camera movement, composition doing all the work, living-picture stillness. For motion: completely locked-off camera.
items.definition: A static locked-off shot plants the camera on a heavy tripod with zero camera movement. Composition, blocking, and duration do the work; the frame is a living picture that does not tour.

items.name: Dolly Zoom
items.prompt: Dolly zoom on [Subject], camera dollies in while the lens zooms out so the figure stays the same size as the background warps, vertigo spatial contradiction, sickly perspective stretch. For motion: dolly zoom on [Subject]: the camera dollies while the lens counter-zooms so the subject size holds and the background warps.
items.definition: A dolly zoom combines camera movement and opposite zooming to preserve subject size while distorting perspective. It is not a zoom with a digital background stretch: translation and focal length work against each other.

items.name: Dutch Roll
items.prompt: Slow roll of the camera on its lens axis around [Subject], horizon rotating from level into a Dutch angle, the world itself tilting. For motion: the camera slowly rolls, tilting the horizon around [Subject] into a Dutch angle.
items.definition: A Dutch roll rotates the camera around the lens axis over time, so a level horizon becomes a canted one. Unease arrives as a move, not as a frozen Dutch still.

items.name: Camera Roll
items.prompt: Full camera roll around [Subject], the frame rotating as if the world has lost its up, disorientation or dance-floor physics. For motion: the camera rolls continuously around its lens axis with [Subject] in frame.
items.definition: A camera roll rotates the frame around the lens axis as if the world has lost its up, either by rolling the camera or by rotating a room around a weighted body. Gravity becomes optional, which is stronger than a small Dutch cant.

items.name: Double Dolly
items.prompt: Double dolly on [Subject]: subject and camera share one rolling platform so the figure appears to glide, feet skating, Spike Lee floating grammar. For motion: [Subject] and the camera move together on the same dolly, creating a floating glide through the space.
items.definition: A double dolly shot moves performer and camera together on one rolling platform so their relative arrangement stays fixed. The actor appears to glide rather than walk: feet skating, weight transfer absent.

items.name: SnorriCam
items.prompt: SnorriCam body-mounted on [Subject], camera locked to the torso so the face stays pinned while the world sloshes behind, subjective intoxication or panic. For motion: body-mounted camera locked to [Subject]'s torso.
items.definition: A SnorriCam fixes the camera to the performer's body so the body remains stable relative to frame while the world moves. A rig points back at the wearer: the face stays pinned, the environment pitches around it.

items.name: Locked-On
items.prompt: Locked-on move with [Subject], camera glued to one object or face while the environment streams past, as if bolted to a vehicle or a falling body. For motion: the camera stays locked on [Subject] while the environment streams past them.
items.definition: A locked-on shot keeps one object or face glued in frame while the world streams past, as if the camera were bolted to a vehicle, a fall, or a spinning set. The subject is the only stable point.

items.name: Walk and Talk
items.prompt: Walk-and-talk tracking of [Subject] in conversation motion, camera leading or flanking at medium, architecture flowing, West Wing corridor energy. For motion: the camera leads [Subject] walking through a space, holding a moving medium two-shot energy even if one figure.
items.definition: A walk and talk shot moves with speaking people, camera leading or flanking at medium, so information and geography travel together. Architecture flows while a moving two-shot (or a moving single with interruptions) carries the dialogue.

items.name: Hyperlapse
items.prompt: Hyperlapse toward or around [Subject], time compressed, crowds and weather racing, camera advancing in steps that become a glide. For motion: hyperlapse: the camera advances through the space around [Subject] while time is compressed, clouds and traffic racing.
items.definition: A hyperlapse combines time-lapse with significant camera movement through space. Time is compressed while the camera advances in steps that assemble into a glide, so crowds and weather race along a real path.

items.name: Slider Shot
items.prompt: Short slider move across [Subject], 60 to 120 centimeters of lateral travel, product or interview parallax, precise and small. For motion: a short slider move laterally across [Subject], subtle parallax, 6 seconds.
items.definition: A slider shot is a short, precise linear move on a compact rail, often 60 to 120 centimeters. It adds parallax to an interview, product, or lock-off without a full dolly track.

items.name: Lazy Susan
items.prompt: Quote the move, not a mood. Still: Lazy-Susan rotation of [Subject] on a turntable while the camera stays put, or the camera circles a static product, commercial 360 hero.
items.definition: A lazy susan shot rotates the subject on a motorized turntable while the camera stays put, or the camera circles at a fixed product-hero radius. Distance holds, so scale does not change, and the far wall barely shears if the disc is what turns.

items.name: Bolt Cam
items.prompt: Name the strike, the rig, and the freeze. Still: Bolt-cam strike toward [Subject], ultra-high-speed camera on a crash rig, the lens hurled at an impact then freezing, sports and music-video violence.
items.definition: A bolt cam hurls an ultra-high-speed camera along a crash rig toward an impact, then freezes. The punch is physical translation on a rail or pneumatic throw, not a change of focal length.

items.name: Aerial
items.prompt: Name height, the map, and the small anchor. Still: Aerial of [Subject] from a high flying camera, geography readable as a map, scale first, the figure small in land or city.
items.definition: An aerial shot views a large area from a high flying camera so geography reads as a map, the figure small in land or city. Helicopter, drone, or a virtual path can carry it; altitude and a stable horizon are the facts.

items.name: Arc
items.prompt: Name the curve, the facing, and how much of the circle. Still: Arc around [Subject], camera traveling a curve while facing them, background sliding, a quarter or half orbit.
items.definition: An arc shot moves the camera around the subject along part of a circle while the lens stays aimed at them. A quarter or half orbit is enough: the axis of the scene changes without a cut, and the background slides.

items.name: Choreo
items.prompt: Name the shared phrase and stop there. Still: Choreographed camera with [Subject], bodies and lens timed together, one phrase of movement, dance-floor blocking.
items.definition: A choreographed camera times bodies and lens as one phrase of movement. The blocking is scored: steps, turns, and the support share a count, then the phrase ends.

items.name: Conveyor
items.prompt: Name the belt and the constant speed. Still: Conveyor move past [Subject], the world sliding on a belt, factory or infinite product line, relentless lateral travel.
items.definition: A conveyor camera treats the world as a belt: relentless lateral travel at constant speed, factory or infinite product-line geometry. The subject can stand still while the line delivers the next unit past the frame.

items.name: Dolly
items.prompt: Say the body travels. Still: Dolly toward or beside [Subject], camera body traveling on a smooth path, true parallax, not a zoom.
items.definition: A dolly shot places the camera on a wheeled platform so the body translates through space: doorway dolly, Fisher, Chapman. Because the nodal point moves, foreground, mid-ground, and background change in parallax, which a zoom cannot do.

items.name: Falling
items.prompt: Name the drop and the ground. Still: Falling camera with [Subject], the lens dropping through air, weight, and wind, a body or viewpoint in free fall.
items.definition: A falling camera drops the lens through air with weight and wind, a body or viewpoint in free fall. Gravity is the path: the ground rises, air rushes, and the horizon may not stay polite.

items.name: Fixed Cam
items.prompt: Lock it. Still: Fixed camera on [Subject], locked position and tilt, all motion belonging to the world, not the operator.
items.definition: A fixed camera locks position and tilt so all motion belongs to the world, not the operator. The mount does not pan, tilt, or travel; blocking has to finish the shot.

items.name: Omnidirectional
items.prompt: Name the sphere and the lack of off-screen. Still: Omnidirectional capture of [Subject], a world that can look every way, spherical space, no off-screen.
items.definition: Omnidirectional capture uses a 360 camera to record spherical space, so the viewer can look any way and there is no behind the camera. Off-screen ceases to exist as a hiding place.

items.name: Pan
items.prompt: Plant the feet. Still: Pan across [Subject], camera rotating on its vertical axis from a fixed point, a horizontal sweep of the world.
items.definition: A pan shot rotates the camera horizontally around a fixed position, yaw on the vertical axis, feet planted. The support does not travel; the horizon should stay level as the frame sweeps the world.

items.name: Parallax
items.prompt: Name near, mid, and far, and make them disagree in speed. Still: Parallax around [Subject], near things racing, far things crawling, depth proven by relative speed.
items.definition: Parallax cinematography is the relative apparent motion between near and far objects as the camera translates. Near things race, far things crawl; that speed difference is how the image proves the world has layers.

items.name: Pass Through
items.prompt: Name the barrier and the far side. Still: Pass-through of [Subject], the camera traveling through a wall, a body, a window as if matter were optional.
items.definition: A camera pass through travels through a wall, a body, or a window as if matter were optional. The path is continuous: one side of the barrier, its thickness, then the next space, without a cut.

items.name: Tilt
items.prompt: Plant the tripod. Still: Tilt on [Subject], camera rotating on its horizontal axis, climbing or descending the world from a fixed point.
items.definition: A tilt shot rotates the camera vertically around a fixed position, pitch on the horizontal axis, tripod planted. Height is revealed or hidden by angle, not by lifting the support.

items.name: Trucking
items.prompt: Name the side-on travel. Still: Trucking with [Subject], lateral dolly, the camera sliding sideways, a sidewalk or corridor peeling by.
items.definition: A trucking shot is a lateral dolly: the camera slides sideways with a walker, a sidewalk or corridor peeling by. Subject size holds; the world streams along the street axis.

items.name: Wandering
items.prompt: Write discovery, not a target lock. Still: Wandering camera near [Subject], unmotivated drift that becomes curiosity, a search without a target yet.
items.definition: A wandering camera drifts near the subject as curiosity, a search without a target yet. The move is not a motivated reframe to a known fact; looking itself is the action until something is found.

items.name: Zoom
items.prompt: Keep the body still. Still: Zoom on [Subject], optical magnification, camera body still, space flattening or opening without parallax.
items.definition: A zoom shot changes focal length without moving the camera. Space flattens or opens with no parallax: near and far grow or shrink together because the nodal point stays put.

items.name: Eyes In
items.prompt: Name the travel and the end state. Still: Eyes-in push on [Subject], the camera traveling into the gaze until the irises own the frame, a portrait that becomes an interior.
items.definition: An eyes in camera push travels into the gaze until the irises own the frame. It does not stop at a close-up; the portrait becomes an interior of sclera, iris, and catchlight.

items.name: Mouth In
items.prompt: Demand the camera end past the lips. Still: Mouth-in move on [Subject], the camera entering speech or appetite, lips as landscape.
items.definition: A mouth in camera move enters speech or appetite until lips and teeth become the set. The camera travels past the portrait into the orifice as landscape.

items.name: Eating Zoom
items.prompt: Crash, food, hold. Still: Eating zoom on [Subject], a crash into the bite, chopsticks or spoon as the last foreground, appetite as a punch-in.
items.definition: An eating zoom is a crash into the bite, chopsticks or spoon as the last foreground, appetite as a punch-in. The move is optical and short; the dish should be nameable in the last frame.

items.name: Buckle Up
items.prompt: Lock to the cabin. Still: Buckle-up camera with [Subject] in a vehicle, the lens strapped to the cabin, acceleration as the grammar, road rushing past.
items.definition: A buckle up camera straps the lens to the cabin with the subject, so the vehicle is the tripod and acceleration is the grammar. Interior stays sharp; the world streaks past the glass.

items.name: Car Chasing
items.prompt: Two vehicles, matched speed. Still: Car-chase coverage of [Subject], pursuit from a second vehicle, matching speed, road as the set.
items.definition: Car chase cinematography covers pursuit from a second vehicle, matching speed, the road as the set. Two machines stay in a line of action; this is the hunter's lens, not a locked interior.

items.name: Car Grip
items.prompt: Show the mount's privilege. Still: Car-grip mount on [Subject]'s vehicle, hood or door as the rig, chrome and asphalt in one plane.
items.definition: A car mount camera bolts to hood, door, or bumper so bodywork sits in the near plane and asphalt slides underneath. Chrome and road share one rigid relationship because the rig is the machine.

items.name: Road Rush
items.prompt: Get down. Still: Road-rush of [Subject], low to the asphalt, speed as smear, headlights and lane lines as weapons.
items.definition: A road rush camera sits low to the asphalt, speed as smear, headlights and lane lines as weapons. The road is the subject; a vehicle is optional.

items.name: Flying Cam Transition
items.prompt: Name the threshold and the landing. Still: Flying-cam transition through [Subject]'s world, one continuous flight that punches a wall or window and lands in a new room.
items.definition: A flying cam transition is one continuous flight that punches a wall or window and lands in a new room. Architecture becomes a tunnel; the join is travel, not a hidden cut.

items.name: Through Object In
items.prompt: Name the object and the arrival. Still: Through-object-in on [Subject], the camera entering via a cup, keyhole, speaker, or mouth, matter as a door.
items.definition: Through object in sends the camera into a cup, keyhole, speaker, or mouth, matter as a door, then arrives on the subject. Scale often changes along a coherent 3D route that a physical camera could not take.

items.name: Through Object Out
items.prompt: Start on the subject, name the object, arrive larger. Still: Through-object-out from [Subject], the camera exiting via an object into a wider world, the interior becoming exterior.
items.definition: Through object out leaves the subject by traveling out through an object into a wider world, interior becoming exterior. The viewpoint can abandon the person and let the decisive event happen off its direct attention.

items.name: Super Dolly In
items.prompt: Long, fast, parallax. Still: Super dolly in on [Subject], a long aggressive travel that eats the room, parallax violent, the face arriving too fast.
items.definition: A super dolly in is a long aggressive travel that eats the room, parallax violent, the face arriving too fast. It is a dolly in stretched until geography collapses into a close-up in one move.

items.name: Super Dolly Out
items.prompt: Long reverse, geography wins. Still: Super dolly out from [Subject], a long retreat that dumps the person into geography, the room exploding open.
items.definition: A super dolly out is a long retreat that dumps the person into geography, the room exploding open. The environment takes the frame; the figure is left inside a system they no longer fill.

items.name: Dolly Zoom In
items.prompt: Write both halves. Still: Dolly zoom in on [Subject], counter-zoom so the figure grows while the background warps inward, vertigo as approach.
items.definition: A dolly zoom in approaches on wheels while the lens zooms out, so the figure holds or grows as the background warps inward. Counter-zoom is the point: size and space disagree.

items.name: Dolly Zoom Out
items.prompt: Dolly out, zoom in. Still: Dolly zoom out on [Subject], the figure shrinking or holding while space yawns, a retreat that stretches the room.
items.definition: A dolly zoom out retreats on wheels while the lens zooms in, the figure shrinking or holding while space yawns. The background stretches away; the face can stay as the room leaves.

items.name: YoYo Zoom
items.prompt: In then out, one breath. Still: Yo-yo zoom on [Subject], in and out on the same axis, a punch then a release, optical breathing.
items.definition: A yoyo zoom inhales and exhales on the optical axis: a punch then a release, camera body still. One breath, two directions, no dolly.

items.name: Rapid Zoom In
items.prompt: Faster than a crash, then hold. Still: Rapid zoom in on [Subject], faster than a polite crash, almost a cut, the world snapping tight.
items.definition: A rapid zoom in snaps focal length faster than a polite crash, almost a cut, the world tightening in a few frames, then a hold. The camera body does not travel.

items.name: Rapid Zoom Out
items.prompt: Snap to wide, hold. Still: Rapid zoom out from [Subject], the environment exploding into view in a snap.
items.definition: A rapid zoom out snaps from the subject to a wide, the environment exploding into view, then holds. Reveal as shock or joke; the camera body still does not travel.

items.name: Head Tracking
items.prompt: Glue to the skull. Still: Head-tracking camera on [Subject], the lens glued to the skull, background sliding as the face stays pinned.
items.definition: A head tracking camera glues the lens to the skull so the face stays pinned while the background orbits. The head is the tripod; turns shear the room.

items.name: Hero Cam
items.prompt: Walk, low, rim. Still: Hero-cam on [Subject], low three-quarter, rim light, a walk that sells myth, comic-book arrival.
items.definition: Hero cam is a low three-quarter tracking walk with rim light, a comic-book arrival at walking speed. The recipe is height plus travel plus a hard edge of light, not a static low angle.

items.name: Robo Arm
items.prompt: Programmed, repeatable, no shake. Still: Robotic arm move around [Subject], programmed path, inhuman precision, product or stunt geometry.
items.definition: A robotic camera arm runs a programmed path with inhuman precision, repeatable every take for product geometry or a stunt match. No operator shake; the spline is the performance.

items.name: Wiggle
items.prompt: Two nearby viewpoints. Still: Wiggle cam on [Subject], tiny stereo rock, a living postcard, depth as a fidget.
items.definition: A wiggle camera rocks between two nearby viewpoints, a tiny stereo fidget that makes a lock-off read as a living postcard. Travel is centimeters, not a dolly.

items.name: 3D Rotation
items.prompt: Turntable of space, figure as object. Still: 3D rotation around [Subject], a turntable of space, the figure as a sculptural object in orbit.
items.definition: A 3d rotation camera treats the figure as a sculptural object on a virtual turntable of space. The world may be a cyc or a void; the point is every side, not a street orbit.

items.name: Crane Over The Head
items.prompt: End almost overhead. Still: Crane over the head of [Subject], the arm rising until the camera looks nearly straight down, a person becoming a map.
items.definition: A crane over the head rises on the arm until the camera looks nearly straight down, a person becoming a map. The end state is overhead, not a high three-quarter.

items.name: Earth Zoom
items.prompt: Satellite to face, one axis. Still: Earth zoom into [Subject], satellite to street in one rush, the planet collapsing into a face.
items.definition: An earth zoom is a continuous or apparently continuous rush from satellite scale down to a face, continent to street to person. Nested geography collapses along one axis; a smooth zoom is not proof of real travel speed.

items.name: Jib Down
items.prompt: Short arm, sit down. Still: Jib down onto [Subject], a short descending arm, intimate arrival, nearby foreground sliding as the camera sits down.
items.definition: A jib down camera is a short descending arm, a few feet of boom, intimate arrival with nearby foreground sliding as the camera sits down. It is a small crane, not a city-scale drop.

items.name: Jib Up
items.prompt: Short rise, room returns. Still: Jib up from [Subject], a short rising arm, the table or face giving the room back, human-scale lift.
items.definition: A jib up camera is a short rising arm that gives a table or face back to the room, human-scale lift. Who else is present appears; a skyline does not have to.

items.name: Extreme Close-Up
items.prompt: Lead with the crop, then the feature. Example: Extreme close-up of [Subject], a single feature filling the frame, pores and texture, tighter than forehead-to-chin.
items.definition: An extreme close-up, or extreme close up shot, fills the frame with one small feature: an eye, a mouth, a fingertip, a trigger. Surrounding space disappears; the crop is tighter than a whole face.

items.name: Choker Shot
items.prompt: Quote the crop. Example: Choker shot of [Subject] from hairline to chin, almost no background.
items.definition: A choker shot, also called a big close-up (BCU), frames the face from hairline to chin, often clipping the skull on every side. Shoulders are out; almost no background remains.

items.name: Close-Up
items.prompt: Name the anatomy. Example: Tight close-up of [Subject], head and upper shoulders, 75mm, shallow depth of field.
items.definition: A close-up, or close up shot, frames a face tightly enough to privilege detail over surroundings, usually head and upper shoulders. The room becomes secondary; the person still reads as a head, not a fragment.

items.name: Medium Close-Up
items.prompt: Say chest up. Example: Medium close-up of [Subject] from chest up, dialogue distance, shoulders and hands still readable, 65 to 75mm.
items.definition: A medium close-up, or medium close up, usually frames a person from chest or shoulders upward. Dialogue distance remains: face, shoulders, and often a hand at chest height stay readable.

items.name: Medium Shot
items.prompt: Say waist. Example: Medium shot of [Subject] from the waist up, conversational distance, 50mm, gesture and face in balance.
items.definition: A medium shot frames a person from approximately the waist upward, so face and gesture share the rectangle. It is the workhorse size of coverage, sometimes called a waist shot.

items.name: Cowboy Shot
items.prompt: Name mid-thigh and the hands. Example: Cowboy shot of [Subject] framed mid-thigh up, hands visible at the holster line, American shot.
items.definition: A cowboy shot frames a person from mid-thigh or the knees upward so the hands stay in at the holster line. It is also called an American shot or knee shot; it is not a waist shot and not a full figure.

items.name: Full Body
items.prompt: Say head to toe. Example: Full-body shot of [Subject], head to toe, figure complete in frame, environment readable around the silhouette.
items.definition: A full body shot holds a person head to toe, with the figure complete and a readable strip of environment around the silhouette. The person is still the subject; the world is a border, not the owner of the frame.

items.name: Long Shot
items.prompt: Say full figure plus geography. Example: Long shot of [Subject] small in a large environment, full figure plus geography.
items.definition: A long shot in cinematography shows the full subject plus a substantial portion of the environment, so a person sits small in geography. The figure is still locatable as a human; the world is large enough to ignore them.

items.name: Extreme Long Shot
items.prompt: Say speck and name the terrain. Example: Extreme long shot of [Subject] as a speck against vast terrain, infinite depth of field, landscape as the true subject.
items.definition: An extreme long shot makes environment, scale, geography, or isolation dominant over individual detail. A person, if present, is a speck: a scale mark, not a portrait.

items.name: Establishing Shot
items.prompt: Declare place and time. Example: Wide establishing shot of [Subject] and the location at once, time of day and spatial relations declared before coverage begins.
items.definition: An establishing shot introduces or re-establishes location, geography, time of day, or social context. It is a job in the sequence, not a synonym for wide or extreme long shot.

items.name: Master Shot
items.prompt: Demand all blocking. Example: Wide master of [Subject] with all blocking visible, the skeleton of the scene in one continuous frame.
items.definition: A master shot covers the complete dramatic action and the spatial geography of a scene in one setup. It is the skeleton you can play in full, then cut into.

items.name: Two-Shot
items.prompt: Demand two people and the gap. Example: Two-shot of [Subject] with a second figure, the space between them doing narrative work, 50mm.
items.definition: A two-shot, or two shot, frames two principal subjects together so their distance and posture can be compared in one composition. The space between them is part of the sentence.

items.name: Three-Shot
items.prompt: Name three and the triangle. Example: Three-shot of [Subject] in a triangular group, alliances and the odd one out readable in blocking.
items.definition: A three-shot, or three shot, frames three principal subjects together, usually so alliances and the odd one out are readable in the blocking. It is a group sentence of three, not three singles cut together.

items.name: Group Shot
items.prompt: Name the unit and the owner. Example: Group shot containing [Subject] among several figures, ensemble blocking, who owns the frame by position and light.
items.definition: A group shot frames a small ensemble as a relational unit, such as a family, a crew, or a jury. Position, height, and light say who belongs and who dominates.

items.name: Insert Shot
items.prompt: Name the object and the scale. Example: Tight close-up of an object that carries the plot near [Subject]: a glass, a letter, a latch.
items.definition: An insert shot is a close view of a story-relevant detail: an object, a hand action, a screen, or text. It points at the thing that will matter, at real scale.

items.name: Cutaway
items.prompt: Name the exit. Example: Cutaway from [Subject] to a related detail in the same world (a clock, a kettle, a street, a listener), not an insert on the actor.
items.definition: A cutaway shot leaves the primary action for a related detail, observer, or part of the same world. It is used for context, reaction, compression, or continuity repair.

items.name: Reaction Shot
items.prompt: Name receiving. Example: Reaction close-up of [Subject] receiving news they cannot speak yet, the face as the cut.
items.definition: A reaction shot shows a character's response to an event, a line, or an unseen stimulus. The important action is watching; the face (or body) is the cut.

items.name: Over-the-Shoulder Coverage
items.prompt: Name the near shoulder and the far face. Example: Over-the-shoulder framing of [Subject], near shoulder soft in foreground, the far face sharp, looking toward the near shoulder, 180-line held.
items.definition: Over-the-shoulder coverage, or an over the shoulder shot, puts a near shoulder or head in the foreground while the far face stays sharp. Paired reverses preserve relational space.

items.name: Single
items.prompt: Say one person and whether the edges are clean. Example: Clean single of [Subject], one person, no foreground shoulder, the frame belonging entirely to them.
items.definition: A single, in single shot cinematography, is a coverage shot of one principal character, not a one-take scene. A clean single keeps other bodies out; a dirty single lets a shoulder or blur from the partner chew the edge without becoming a true over-the-shoulder.

items.name: Cut-ins
items.prompt: Say already in the master and same axis. Example: Cut-in on a detail of [Subject] already in the master, tighter, the same axis, a fact the wide cannot prove.
items.definition: A cut-in, or cut in shot, moves from a wider view to a closer detail of something already present in that space, usually along the same axis. It proves a fact the wide cannot prove: the hands, the phone, the wound.

items.name: Gesture
items.prompt: Name the movement. Example: Gesture close on [Subject], the meaning in a hand, a glance, a weight shift, coverage of the small action.
items.definition: Gesture cinematography sizes and times a shot around a discrete expressive body movement: a hand, a glance, a weight shift. The plot is in the motion, not in an object sitting still.

items.name: Interview
items.prompt: Lock eyeline and size. Example: Interview frame of [Subject], talking-head distance, eyeline just off lens, a listener implied.
items.definition: Interview cinematography is a talking-head setup: stable size, eyeline just off the lens, a listener implied. Someone is answering a question we often do not hear.

items.name: Product
items.prompt: Name the object as hero. Example: Product hero of [Subject], catalog clarity, controlled reflections, the object as the only subject.
items.definition: Product cinematography lights and frames an object the way a portrait treats a face: hero angle, catalog clarity, controlled reflections. The thing is the subject, not a plot insert in a messy room.

items.name: Video Portraits
items.prompt: Demand the hold. Still: Video portrait of [Subject], a held face, duration as intimacy.
items.definition: A video portrait is a sustained, simply covered study of one person: stable size, patient time, the face as the whole event. Duration is the intimacy; a person is enough.

items.name: Wide Shot
items.prompt: Say full environment and small bodies. Example: Wide shot of [Subject] in full environment, bodies small enough that place still speaks.
items.definition: A wide shot shows the subject in full environment, with bodies small enough that place still speaks. It is environment-forward coverage: do not isolate yet.

items.name: Eye Level
items.prompt: When to use it Use it for a conversation that should not take sides, or for a face you want believed without the camera lobbying. Concrete beat: two adults at a kitchen table, seated eyes matched, no ceiling grab.
items.definition: An eye-level shot places the camera at the subject's eye height with a horizontal sightline and a level horizon. It is the default equal relationship: height and tilt assign no rank until you leave this setup.

items.name: High Angle
items.prompt: Name the look-down, not only camera up high. Quote: High-angle shot looking down on [Subject], the figure diminished, architecture or sky weighing on them.
items.definition: A high-angle shot looks downward at the subject from above eye level, an oblique pitch rather than a straight drop. More floor enters the frame, the figure occupies less of the rectangle, and the viewpoint reads as observation from above.

items.name: Low Angle
items.prompt: Name the look-up and the ceiling. Quote: Low-angle shot looking up at [Subject], converging verticals, heroic or oppressive height, Citizen Kane floor.
items.definition: A low-angle shot looks upward at the subject from below eye level, so verticals converge and ceilings or sky take weight. The camera is not merely low; it is pitched up, and that pitch is what assigns monument or intimidation.

items.name: Bird's-Eye View
items.prompt: Lock height and pitch. Quote: Bird's-eye view straight down on [Subject], camera over one seated person and a table, floor as a map, no extra limbs.
items.definition: A bird's-eye view shot looks steeply or directly down from a great height so people and furniture become a map. Height, not just distance, is the point of view: life reads as a board game or a ritual seen from above.

items.name: Worm's-Eye View
items.prompt: Say straight up, not merely low. Quote: Worm's-eye view from ground level looking straight up at [Subject], extreme low, verticals collapsing inward, awe or terror.
items.definition: A worm's-eye view looks sharply upward from ground level or below the subject, an extreme low pitch that collapses verticals inward. The subject is a tower and the camera is dust.

items.name: Overhead Top-Down
items.prompt: Lock 90 degrees and the rectangle. Quote: Overhead top-down shot of [Subject] at 90 degrees, flat-lay or room plan, shadows as drawing.
items.definition: An overhead top-down shot looks nearly straight down at 90 degrees, flattening bodies and spaces into a graphic arrangement. Faces are scarce; silhouette, props, and the plan of the table or room do the talking.

items.name: Ground Level
items.prompt: Name the floor as foreground. Quote: Ground-level camera looking steeply up at [Subject], lens nearly on the floor, boots and trailing coat monumental.
items.definition: A ground-level shot puts the lens almost on the floor, so boots, hems, wheels, and the dirt become actors. Height is the fact: the camera starts from the ground plane, whether it looks along the street or steeply up.

items.name: Dutch Angle
items.prompt: Name the roll in degrees and keep the buildings straight. Quote: Dutch angle of [Subject], camera rolled 20 to 30 degrees, diagonal horizon, moral or mental tilt.
items.definition: A Dutch angle rolls the camera so verticals and the horizon appear tilted. The cant is usually static: gravity's down is no longer the bottom of the frame, which is why the world reads as off its axis.

items.name: Point of View
items.prompt: Describe the seen world, not the seer. Quote: What [Subject] sees: the world at their eye height, no back of a head, no shoulder of the looker in frame.
items.definition: A POV shot makes the camera function as a character's optical viewpoint: what they see at their eye height. The looker's head and shoulder stay out of the frame; we inhabit the look, not a seat behind it.

items.name: Profile
items.prompt: Lock the yaw. Quote: True profile of [Subject], camera at 90 degrees to the head, one ear, the nose as architecture, looking offscreen.
items.definition: A profile shot places the camera at 90 degrees to the head so one ear, the jaw, and the nose read as architecture, with the look offscreen. It is a true side view, not a three-quarter face and not a stamped coin if the living head still breathes.

items.name: Three-Quarter Angle
items.prompt: Name the turn in degrees and keep both eyes. Quote: Three-quarter angle on [Subject], face turned about 45 degrees, classic portrait dimensionality.
items.definition: A three-quarter angle turns the face about 45 degrees to the camera so both eyes remain visible and the far cheek recedes. It is the standard narrative portrait angle: dimensionality without a full front or a true side.

items.name: Reverse Angle
items.prompt: Describe both poles even if you generate one still. Quote: Reverse angle on [Subject], the opposing view of a dialogue or standoff, 180-line respected, geography flipping.
items.definition: A reverse-angle shot views the same spatial relationship from the opposing side, completing the axis of a look, a dialogue, or a standoff. Geography flips; the 180-degree line is respected so screen direction still matches.

items.name: Trunk Shot
items.prompt: The rim is mandatory. Quote: Trunk shot looking up at [Subject] from inside a car trunk or similar confined pit, playful low-angle signature.
items.definition: A trunk shot places the camera inside a car trunk or similar confined pit, looking up at the people who open it, with the lid and rim framing their downward looks. It is a located low viewpoint, not a generic look-up in a parking lot.

items.name: Hip Level
items.prompt: Name belt height, not low camera. Quote: Hip-level camera on [Subject], gunbelt height, Western stance, hands and holster in the plane of focus.
items.definition: A hip-level shot sits the camera around belt or holster height so hands, gait, and weapons share the plane of focus. It is a height choice, usually with a level horizon: the hands will decide.

items.name: Shoulder Level
items.prompt: Separate height from move. Quote: Shoulder-level camera on [Subject], slightly below the eyes, a walking companion's view, less formal than true eye-level.
items.definition: A shoulder-level camera sits slightly below the eyes, at the height of a walking companion. It is less formal than true eye level and less monumental than a low angle; the face is still the target, seen from the deltoid rather than the pupil.

items.name: First-Person
items.prompt: Require a body at the edges. Quote: First-person camera as [Subject] would see, hands entering frame, breath, a body that owns the lens.
items.definition: A first-person camera makes the lens function as a character's bodily viewpoint, with a body that owns it: hands entering the frame, breath, tools, locomotion. It is subjective seeing as continuous embodiment, not a single optical insert.

items.name: Fourth Wall
items.prompt: The eyeline is the law. Quote: Fourth-wall look from [Subject], eyes into the lens, the scene admitting an audience.
items.definition: A fourth-wall look aims the subject's eyes into the taking lens, so the scene admits an audience. The camera is no longer an invisible observer; it is a person in the room, or the spectator the character has decided to include.

items.name: Object POV
items.prompt: Name the object and keep it fixed in frame. Quote: Object POV as if [Subject] were seen from a tool, a ball, a bullet, a phone: the thing looking.
items.definition: An object-POV shot is the viewpoint of a tool, a ball, a bullet, a phone, or a vehicle: the prop has eyes. The camera is parented to that object, so the object stays stable in the frame while the world moves relative to it.

items.name: Incline
items.prompt: Give a small number. Quote: Inclined camera on [Subject], a gentle cant, not a full Dutch, the floor suggesting slope or unease.
items.definition: An incline is a slight camera roll, a gentle cant of the floor rather than a full Dutch angle. The horizon is a few degrees off true, enough to suggest slope or unease without declaring that the world has fallen over.

items.name: Three-Point Lighting
items.prompt: Name all three jobs, not the word portrait. " Add key side (left or right), fill ratio, and backlight color.
items.definition: Three-point lighting, the basic three point lighting setup, places a key, a fill, and a backlight so a face is modeled from one dominant side, opened in the shadows, and separated from the background. The key is brightest and sets direction; fill and back exist only as ratios against it.

items.name: Key Light
items.prompt: Name the source and the side before any style word. " Add height (high, eye, table), hardness, and Kelvin.
items.definition: A key light in key light cinematography is the principal source that sets the subject's dominant direction, shape, and exposure. Shadows fall away from it; every other light is measured against it.

items.name: Fill Light
items.prompt: Say which cheek opens and how little. " Add 2:1 or 4:1 if you need a number.
items.definition: Fill light reduces contrast or adds detail in areas the key does not reach, usually from the opposite side and at a lower level. It is a ratio tool, not a second sun.

items.name: Backlight
items.prompt: Put the source behind the body, not on the nose. " Name hair, coat edge, and whether haze is present.
items.definition: Backlight in backlight cinematography is light coming from behind the subject toward the camera, tracing edges and lifting the figure off the background. It may stay a thin rim or, in haze, become a visible shaft.

items.name: Rim Light
items.prompt: Forbid the cartoon stroke. Use: "Photographic backlight on [Subject] from behind, a thin natural highlight on hat brim, hair, and coat edge, faces staying dark.
items.definition: Rim lighting is a narrow edge of light, usually from a flagged backlight, that separates a subject from the background without opening the face. The highlight sits on brim, hair, and coat; flesh stays mostly dark.

items.name: Kicker
items.prompt: Localize the highlight. Use: "A small warm lamp behind and to the side of [Subject], a thin highlight on the far jaw and coat shoulder only.
items.definition: A kicker light is a relatively hard side-back accent on cheek, jaw, shoulder, or an object edge, placed behind and to one side of the subject. It is a slice, not a full wrap and not a hair-only rim.

items.name: Hair Light
items.prompt: Aim at the crown, not the nose. Use: "A small lamp behind and above [Subject], lighting only the top of the hair as a rim.
items.definition: A hair light is a small source behind and above the subject that lights only the top of the hair as a rim so texture separates from the background. The face stays on the key or in cooler shadow.

items.name: Eye Light
items.prompt: Specify a reflection, not a glow. Use: "A dark portrait of [Subject], face mostly in shadow, a tiny white reflection of a lamp sitting in each human iris.
items.definition: An eye light in eye light cinematography is a small frontal source used to put a catchlight in the irises or to lift the eyes a fraction without becoming a fill. The face can stay in shadow; the eyes remain human, not lamps.

items.name: High-Key Lighting
items.prompt: Ask for low contrast and protected whites, not a flash. " Add large sources and say highlights hold texture.
items.definition: High-key lighting, or high key lighting, uses relatively low contrast, bright exposure, and limited deep shadow so the frame stays open and readable. It is a contrast ratio, not a command to overexpose.

items.name: Low-Key Lighting
items.prompt: Name the pool and the black. " Name the single source and forbid extra fill.
items.definition: Low-key lighting, or low key lighting, uses high contrast, selective illumination, and substantial shadow so most of the frame can sit near black. One pool of light is often enough; the dark is designed, not an accident of underexposure.

items.name: Chiaroscuro
items.prompt: One source, fast falloff, modeled planes. " Name the lamp.
items.definition: Chiaroscuro lighting uses strong light-dark contrast to model volume and to create moral, psychological, or dramatic tension. Darkness withholds; the lit plane is what the scene will admit.

items.name: Rembrandt Lighting
items.prompt: Demand the triangle by name. " Say the nose shadow connects to the cheek shadow.
items.definition: Rembrandt lighting, in rembrandt lighting terms, is a portrait pattern in which the key sits high and about 45 degrees off axis so the nose shadow joins the shadow cheek, leaving a small triangle of light under the shadow-side eye. The rest of that cheek stays dark.

items.name: Butterfly Lighting
items.prompt: Keep the key on center and high. " Forbid a shadow cheek.
items.definition: Butterfly lighting, also called Paramount lighting, places the key high and on the camera axis so a small butterfly-shaped shadow falls under the nose on the philtrum. Both cheeks stay open; both eyes take light.

items.name: Loop Lighting
items.prompt: Name the loop and forbid the triangle. Use: "Loop lighting on [Subject], key slightly off-axis, a small loop shadow from the nose toward the corner of the mouth." Add that the loop does not touch the cheek shadow.
items.definition: Loop lighting creates a small nose shadow that loops toward the corner of the mouth and does not connect to the cheek shadow. The key sits slightly off axis and a little high, a middle step between butterfly and Rembrandt.

items.name: Split Lighting
items.prompt: Demand the vertical cut. Use: "Split lighting on [Subject], one half of the face in light, the other in shadow, a vertical moral cut." Add key at 90 degrees, almost no fill, no triangle on the dark cheek.
items.definition: Split lighting divides the face into a lit half and a shadow half by placing the key at about 90 degrees to the nose, a vertical cut down the center line. There is no Rembrandt triangle and no loop; the far plane is largely gone.

items.name: Short Lighting
items.prompt: Name which cheek is near. Use: "Short lighting on [Subject], the side turned away from camera is keyed, the near side falls toward shadow, slimming and dramatic." Add that the camera-facing cheek is the darker one.
items.definition: Short lighting in short lighting terms keys the side of the face turned away from camera, so the camera sees more shadow than light. The head looks slimmer and more dimensional because the near cheek falls off.

items.name: Broad Lighting
items.prompt: Light the near cheek. Use: "Broad lighting on [Subject], the camera-facing side keyed, open and public, less shadow on the near cheek." Say the bright plane is the one occupying most of the frame.
items.definition: Broad lighting keys the side of the face turned toward camera, so the near cheek is the bright one and the shadow sits on the far side. The face reads open, public, and less mysterious.

items.name: Silhouette
items.prompt: Expose the ground, starve the body. " Name a readable outline (limbs separated).
items.definition: A silhouette shot places the subject dark against a brighter background so the figure reads as shape, not as a modeled face. Gesture and contour do the work; surface detail is gone.

items.name: Motivated Lighting
items.prompt: Justify every beam. " Name the story source, its side, hardness, and Kelvin.
items.definition: Motivated lighting is designed to appear consistent with a visible or plausible story-world source: a window, a lamp, a sign, the sky. Hidden units may exist, but they match that source in direction, hardness, and color.

items.name: Practical Lighting
items.prompt: Show the lamp and let it work. Use: "Practical lighting on [Subject] from visible lamps, neon, candles, or screens in frame, mixed color temperatures, no hidden movie lights." Name which fixture is the key and its color.
items.definition: Practical lighting uses a visible or logically present light source within the set as a real contributor: lamps, neon, candles, screens. You see the fixture, and it (or a unit matching it) actually lights the face.

items.name: Available Light
items.prompt: Forbid added units. " Name the hour and the existing source.
items.definition: Available light in available light cinematography is the illumination already at the location before the crew adds or changes units: sun, sky, or existing interior fixtures. You commit to the hour and the existing contrast.

items.name: Naturalistic Ambient
items.prompt: Ask for room tone, not a named portrait pattern. " Name a window side.
items.definition: Naturalistic ambient lighting wraps the subject in soft, directionally plausible room or sky tone so the craft reads as unstyled even when units are added. Shadows stay believable; nothing announces a movie lamp.

items.name: Bounce Light
items.prompt: Name the reflecting surface. " State the wall's side and color.
items.definition: Bounce lighting reflects light from a surface (wall, ceiling, poly, card) before it reaches the subject, so the apparent source becomes that large surface. Direction remains, but shadow edges soften and wrap.

items.name: Hard Light
items.prompt: Name a small distant source and razor edges. Use: "Hard light on [Subject] from a small distant source, razor shadow edges, texture amplified, noir graphic." Forbid silks, wrap, and cloudy softness unless weather is the point.
items.definition: Hard light in hard light cinematography comes from a small apparent source and produces crisp shadow edges and specular definition on skin, metal, and walls. Texture is amplified; falloff can still be steep or long depending on distance.

items.name: Soft Light
items.prompt: Name a large source and gentle edges. " Keep a key side.
items.definition: Soft light in soft light cinematography comes from a large apparent source and produces gradual shadow transitions and wrap around the face or body. Speculars get larger and dimmer; texture is reduced.

items.name: Side Lighting
items.prompt: Put the lamp at 90 degrees. " Name hardness.
items.definition: Side lighting keys primarily from one side, around 90 degrees to the camera-subject line, so shape and texture are emphasized. Half the form goes toward light, half toward shadow.

items.name: Top Light
items.prompt: Put the lamp on the ceiling axis. Use: "A lamp directly above [Subject], light falling on forehead and shoulders, eye sockets in shadow, human eyes, no light emitting from the pupils." Forbid frontal beauty fill.
items.definition: Top lighting is illumination from directly above the subject, falling on forehead, nose bridge, and shoulders while the eye sockets and the underside of the chin go into shadow. The source is a ceiling, a rig, or a high practical, not a frontal beauty key.

items.name: Underlighting
items.prompt: Put the source under the chin. Use: "A lamp on the table below [Subject]'s chin, pointing up.
items.definition: Underlighting, also called uplighting, lights from below the face so shadows climb the cheekbones and the tops of the eye sockets. The modeling is the reverse of daylight and often reads as uncanny.

items.name: Cross Lighting
items.prompt: Name two opposing keys. " Specify colors if they differ.
items.definition: Cross lighting keys subjects from opposite side directions, so each person or each side of a body gets a key and a far rim. It is common in dialogue coverage, stage, and concert work.

items.name: Window Light
items.prompt: Make the window the only key. Use: "Window light as the only key on [Subject], large soft directional source, falloff into the room, painterly interior." Name which wall holds the glass and whether the sky is overcast or late sun.
items.definition: Window light in window light cinematography is illumination shaped to appear as light entering through a window: a large, directional source with falloff into the room. The architecture is the modifier.

items.name: Candlelight
items.prompt: Keep the flame small and close. " Cluster the candles, kill electric fill, and let corners go dark.
items.definition: Candlelight in candlelight cinematography is a small warm practical or a simulated flame with rapid falloff, often around 1800K, that carves faces near the flame and lets the rest of the room die. Flicker is part of the source, not a grade.

items.name: Neon Practicals
items.prompt: Make the signs the keys. " Name which tube hits which cheek.
items.definition: Neon practicals are visible neon or similar sign tubes used as actual keys or strong accents, coloring the subject with magenta, cyan, or other tube hues instead of a hidden white source. The city fixture is the lamp.

items.name: Golden Hour
items.prompt: Keep the sun low and real. " Say the sun is just above the horizon.
items.definition: Golden hour in golden hour cinematography is low-angle warm sunlight shortly after sunrise or before sunset, when the sun is near the horizon. Shadows go long; the light is directional, warm, and brief.

items.name: Blue Hour
items.prompt: Keep the sky luminous and cool. Use: "Blue hour wrap on [Subject], deep cobalt sky still glowing, warm practicals kicking in." Forbid a visible sun disk and a black night sky with no residual light.
items.definition: Blue hour in blue hour cinematography is cool ambient twilight before sunrise or after sunset, when the sun is below the horizon but the sky still glows. There is no hard sunlight; the sky is a large cool source, and warm practicals often kick in.

items.name: Dappled Light
items.prompt: Name the obstruction. Use: "Sun through leaves on [Subject], irregular patches of brightness and leaf-shaped shadows on coat and horse, a real tree overhead." Forbid a clean unpatterned key and a venetian-bar prison graphic unless blinds are the story.
items.definition: Dappled light is broken patches of brightness and shadow caused by foliage, water, blinds, or another irregular obstruction in a hard beam. The pattern is organic and often moving.

items.name: Gobo Lighting
items.prompt: Name the object in the beam. " Specify a hard source.
items.definition: Gobo lighting places a pattern or object in a light beam (a gobo or cucoloris) so the source throws graphic shadows across face, body, and wall. The room writes on the person.

items.name: Volumetric Light
items.prompt: Name source plus medium. " Attach every beam to a window, sun, or searchlight.
items.definition: Volumetric lighting makes beams visible through haze, fog, dust, smoke, or other particles, so the air photographs as well as the subject. Also called god rays or crepuscular rays when the shafts are distinct.

items.name: Cameo Lighting
items.prompt: Kill the room. " Keep the face modeled.
items.definition: Cameo lighting isolates a lit subject against a predominantly dark environment, so the figure sits in a pool and the world falls to black. The person remains modeled; the set is withheld.

items.name: Epiphany
items.prompt: Write the before and after. Still: "Epiphany light on [Subject], a sudden intelligible brightness, as if the thought itself switched a lamp." Video: "Light finds [Subject] as a realization lands, the face becoming the brightest fact in the room." Name what caused the change (sun, door, lamp).
items.definition: Epiphany lighting is a change of illumination that makes a face or figure suddenly the brightest readable fact in the room as a realization lands. The light finds the person; it is timed to understanding, not left as a static setup.

items.name: Spotlight
items.prompt: Demand a hard pool and a dark surround. " Mention a visible circle or shuttered edge.
items.definition: A spotlight in spotlight cinematography is a focused, hard-edged pool from a theatrical or similar instrument, with darkness around the circle. The person is treated as an act inside that pool.

items.name: Glam
items.prompt: Sell the face with physics, not a mood word. Use: "Soft beauty key on [Subject], large source, catchlights inside the eyes, a little diffusion on skin.
items.definition: Glam lighting, in glam lighting terms, is a large beauty key with catchlights in the eyes and a little diffusion on skin, built to sell the face. It is a package of size, frontal or near-frontal placement, and skin treatment, not a single nose-shadow pattern.

items.name: Rule of Thirds
items.prompt: Write the grid, not a mood. Rule-of-thirds placement of [Subject] on a power intersection, horizon on a third, breathing room in the look direction.
items.definition: The rule of thirds in rule of thirds cinematography divides the frame into nine equal cells and parks important masses on those lines or at their four intersections. The horizon usually sits on an upper or lower third so land and sky are not equal partners, and the subject usually sits off-center with look-space in the larger remaining field.

items.name: Golden Ratio
items.prompt: Name the curve and the destination. Golden-ratio spiral composition around [Subject], the eye traveling a harmonic curve rather than a grid.
items.definition: Golden ratio composition organizes the frame with proportional relationships near phi, about eight to five, as a phi grid or a logarithmic spiral rather than a 3x3. The main mass sits closer to center than a third, and the eye is asked to travel a curve through secondary masses instead of jumping cell to cell.

items.name: Central Framing
items.prompt: Name the axis. Central framing of [Subject], the figure on the optical axis, bilateral weight, a formal altar in the frame.
items.definition: Central framing, also called dead center or center punch, places the figure on the optical axis so the body sits on the crosshairs of the frame. Bilateral weight may gather around that body, but the first fact is placement: the person is the altar, not a guest in a third.

items.name: Centered Composition
items.prompt: Ask for the whole altar. Dead-center composition of [Subject], bilateral symmetry or frontal tableau, Wes Anderson formality, the subject as altar.
items.definition: Centered composition places the dominant subject on or near the central vertical axis and organizes the rest of the picture around that axis. The frame reads as a frontal tableau: walls, furniture, and attendants arranged so the subject is an altar, not an accident of blocking.

items.name: Symmetry
items.prompt: Demand the mirror. Perfect symmetry around [Subject], mirrored architecture, a central axis, obsessive order.
items.definition: Symmetry in a symmetrical composition balances visual masses around an axis, usually the vertical centerline, so left answers right. The world looks designed, or it is pretending to be, whether or not a person occupies the middle.

items.name: Asymmetry
items.prompt: Name the offset and the answer. Asymmetrical balance with [Subject] offset, counterweights of color or mass, tension instead of mirror.
items.definition: Asymmetry, or asymmetrical composition, offsets the dominant mass and answers it with a different kind of weight: color, light, a small face, a dark void, or a distant doorway. The frame does not mirror, so leftover space is a counterweight rather than a matching wing.

items.name: Leading Lines
items.prompt: Name the vector and the landing. Leading lines driving the eye to [Subject], rails, corridors, roads, or shadows converging on the figure.
items.definition: Leading lines in leading lines cinematography are edges, rails, roads, corridors, shadows, or gestures that steer the eye toward or through the image. The lines are vectors in the diagram, not decoration around a centered face.

items.name: Frame within Frame
items.prompt: Name both rectangles. Frame-within-frame around [Subject], doorway, window, mirror, or arch as a second rectangle, nested attention.
items.definition: A frame within a frame (doorway framing, surcadrage) puts a second rectangle inside the screen, a door, window, arch, mirror, or gap that encloses the subject. The inner aperture is a second boundary, and crossing it is a beat, not a decoration.

items.name: Negative Space
items.prompt: Say what is empty and where the body sits. Vast negative space around [Subject], the figure small, absence as weight, Antonioni emptiness.
items.definition: Negative space in negative space cinematography leaves a large, relatively empty area around or beside the subject so absence becomes a mass. The unoccupied field is still a world (sky, wall, snow, sea), and the subject occupies a small or unusual portion of the diagram.

items.name: Foreground Interest
items.prompt: Name the near object and whether it is sharp. Strong foreground object between lens and [Subject], dirty aperture of flowers, fence, or glass, layered depth.
items.definition: Foreground interest (a foreground anchor or occluded observation) puts a salient near object between the lens and the subject: flowers, a fence, glass, a table, or a body. The near layer creates depth, scale, a visual entry, or partial concealment, so air and obstacle sit between us and them.

items.name: Layered Depth
items.prompt: Assign jobs to planes. Three-plane composition around [Subject], foreground, mid, and deep background all carrying information, deep staging.
items.definition: Layered depth, or layered composition, stages important action on at least two distances, typically foreground, midground, and background in one picture. Depth staging is that arrangement, while deep focus is a separate optical choice about how much of it is sharp.

items.name: Diagonal Composition
items.prompt: Name the bias line and keep the horizon honest unless you also want a dutch. Diagonal composition through [Subject], energy on the bias, unstable, rain or stairs as the line.
items.definition: Diagonal composition uses diagonal lines and masses (stairs, rifles, rain, a body on the bias, a street receding on a corner) to raise energy, instability, or depth. The camera can stay level, because the set supplies the tilt of the diagram.

items.name: Triangular Composition
items.prompt: Name the three masses and the apex. Triangular arrangement with [Subject] at an apex, three masses locking the frame, Renaissance blocking.
items.definition: Triangular composition arranges subjects or visual masses into a triangle so three points lock the frame. A group gets a hierarchy: the apex is usually power, witness, or the object of desire, and the base is support, threat, or the audience inside the picture.

items.name: Headroom
items.prompt: State tight or open, and what lives in the gap. Deliberate headroom on [Subject], either tight to the hair (pressure) or generously open (air, God, sky).
items.definition: Headroom in headroom cinematography is the space between the crown of the head and the top frame edge. Tight headroom applies pressure, while generous headroom hands the upper field to air, architecture, or sky.

items.name: Lead Room
items.prompt: Name the direction of the surplus. Lead room in front of [Subject]'s look or walk, more space in the direction of attention than behind, forward narrative.
items.definition: Lead room in lead room cinematography (nose room, looking room) is space in the direction a subject looks or moves. More frame sits ahead of the walk or the gaze than behind the head, so the surplus is the path rather than leftover wallpaper.

items.name: Short Siding
items.prompt: Name the crush. Short-sided framing of [Subject], look space crushed, the face near the frame edge they look toward, trapped or urgent.
items.definition: Short siding places the face near the frame edge the character looks toward, crushing look-space and leaving surplus air behind the head. The edge they face becomes a wall, so the diagram denies them a future in the picture.

items.name: Visual Weight
items.prompt: Name the winner and the equalizer. Composition balancing visual weight around [Subject], a bright small thing equal to a large dark mass, scale of attention.
items.definition: Visual weight in visual weight composition is the attention an element attracts through size, contrast, color, position, focus, faces, or motion. A small bright thing can equal a large dark mass, because scale of attention is not scale of object.

items.name: Repetition and Pattern
