items.prompt: Name the unit and the break. Repeating pattern around [Subject], columns, windows, soldiers, a break in the pattern as the story.
items.definition: Repetition and pattern composition repeats shapes, colors, lines, positions, or actions so the eye reads a system of columns, windows, soldiers, or hotel doors. A break in that pattern is often the story, because the grid had already set the expectation.

items.name: Figure-Ground
items.prompt: Name the split method. Clear figure-ground separation of [Subject] from background, contrast of tone, color, or focus so the person reads instantly.
items.definition: Figure-ground composition separates the subject from the field so the person or object reads in under a second. Contrast of tone, color, or focus does the split, and if figure and ground share the same value the diagram fails even if the acting is good.

items.name: Tonal Contrast
items.prompt: Declare which pole the subject occupies. High tonal contrast composition with [Subject] as the lightest or darkest mass, graphic punch, no mid-gray mush.
items.definition: Tonal contrast, the contrast composition of lightest against darkest mass, organizes the frame as a fight of value with the subject as one of those poles. Graphic punch replaces mid-grey mush, so the diagram reads as a poster of value rather than a gentle range of detail.

items.name: One-Point Perspective
items.prompt: Demand a single vanishing point and a square camera. One-point perspective corridor toward [Subject] or through them, vanishing point on axis, Kubrick infinity.
items.definition: One-point perspective in one point perspective cinematography squares the camera to a plane so receding parallels meet at a single vanishing point, often on the central axis. The result is tunnel depth or ceremonial order: a corridor, a nave, a hotel hall aimed at infinity or at a person.

items.name: Vanishing Point
items.prompt: Place the point and the person. Deep vanishing point beyond [Subject], rails or road sucking the eye to infinity, the person as a gate.
items.definition: A vanishing point in vanishing point composition is the apparent meeting place of parallel lines in perspective, a destination for rails, a road, or a colonnade. The person often stands as a gate in front of that meeting, or occupies it as the target of the architecture.

items.name: Dirty Frame
items.prompt: Occupy the edges and name the matter. Dirty frame around [Subject], out-of-focus shoulders, glass, foliage, or crowd chewing the edges, voyeur layers.
items.definition: A dirty frame in dirty frame cinematography lets out-of-focus shoulders, glass, foliage, or crowd chew the edges of the picture so the aperture is occupied. The camera sits inside a populated space, not on a seamless studio axis.

items.name: Clean Frame
items.prompt: Forbid the corners. Clean frame of [Subject], edges empty, no accidental objects, studio-poster clarity, isolation by tidiness.
items.definition: A clean frame in clean frame cinematography keeps the edges empty of accidental objects so isolation arrives by tidiness, not by blur. The diagram has no landlord in the corners, which is studio-poster clarity even on a real street.

items.name: Look Space
items.prompt: Give the gaze a field and keep the object off unless you want it. Generous look space for [Subject], the off-screen gaze owning a field of air, tension in what we cannot see.
items.definition: Look space framing is the field in front of a gaze, the air a look owns, often because the important object is off-screen. In cutting, that look may be joined to what is seen (raccord regard, the look-object relationship).

items.name: Architexture
items.prompt: Let the building win. Architecture as texture around [Subject], facades, grids, and materials filling the frame until the person is a detail of the building.
items.definition: Architexture, a nickname for architectural cinematography that treats the set as subject, fills the frame with facades, grids, and materials until a person is a detail of the building. Texture, module, and mass own space, and the body is an ornament or a scale figure.

items.name: Reflections
items.prompt: Name the surface and both occupants. Reflections of [Subject] in glass, water, or chrome, observer and observed in one plane.
items.definition: Reflections in reflection cinematography put observer and observed in one plane by using glass, water, chrome, or a mirror. Mirror dialogue and one-way-glass staging let two spaces occupy a single composition, because optics, not a filter, do the doubling.

items.name: Screen in Screen
items.prompt: Specify the outer view and the inner picture. Screen-in-screen of [Subject], a monitor, phone, or cinema inside the cinema, nested looking.
items.definition: Screen in screen (desktop film, interface as the camera) nests a monitor, phone, television, or cinema inside the cinema so someone is watching a picture of someone. The inner image has its own crop, delay, and artifacts, and nested looking is the diagram.

items.name: Tableau
items.prompt: Ask for arrangement and a hold. Tableau of [Subject], arranged bodies, a living painting, duration instead of coverage.
items.definition: A tableau (tableau vivant, frontal ensemble, or frieze) is a staged composition whose meaning develops inside a relatively fixed frame. Arranged bodies and objects form a living picture, so duration replaces coverage while the camera stays locked or nearly locked.

items.name: Void
items.prompt: Delete the place. Void around [Subject], darkness or blank field eating the world, a figure against nothing.
items.definition: A void in void cinematography erases the set: darkness, white, or a blank field eating the world until a figure stands against nothing. Negative space still belongs to a place, while a void deletes place, leaving almost no landlord but the body or the darkness that might eat it.

items.name: Voyeur
items.prompt: Name the hide and the forbidden view. Voyeur frame of [Subject], watching from concealment, dirty edges, a view we should not have.
items.definition: Voyeur cinematography places the camera in concealment so the audience is trespassing: a view through foliage, glass, a grate, or a distant window, often with dirty edges. The diagram is a peephole, not coverage, and the owner of that hide does not want us there.

items.name: Windows
items.prompt: Make the panes the subject. Windows as the true subject around [Subject], stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames.
items.definition: Windows cinematography treats panes as the true subject: stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames. The diagram is a grid of possible pictures, not one doorway around one face.

items.name: 14mm Ultra-Wide
items.prompt: Name the stand and the stretch. 14mm ultra-wide on [Subject], exaggerated perspective, looming foreground, stretched architecture, slight heroic distortion.
items.definition: A 14mm ultra-wide in 14mm cinematography is a very short focal length that, from a close stand, takes in a huge field and exaggerates near-to-far size. The close camera position, not the millimeter stamp alone, is what balloons a foreground face or object against a receding room.

items.name: 24mm Wide
items.prompt: Lead with body in space, not with a mood. 24mm wide on [Subject], environmental portrait, body in space, moderate stretch, reportage coverage.
items.definition: A 24mm wide in 24mm lens cinematography is a moderately wide prime that holds a person and a usable amount of place without extreme stretch. Body and architecture share the rectangle; neither fully wins.

items.name: 35mm Moderate Wide
items.prompt: Name the storyteller length and the extra world. 35mm on [Subject], storyteller focal length, natural perspective with a little more world than 50.
items.definition: A 35mm moderate wide in 35mm cinematography is the common narrative wide-normal: natural perspective with a little more world than a 50mm. It is default coverage for scenes that need both face and room.

items.name: 50mm Normal
items.prompt: Name the refusal to stretch or stack. 50mm normal lens on [Subject], human-scale perspective, neither compressed nor stretched, conversational truth.
items.definition: A 50mm normal in 50mm cinematography is the conventional normal prime: from a typical stand it neither stretches near space nor stacks distant planes. The glass refuses to editorialize perspective; camera position still does all of that work.

items.name: 85mm Portrait
items.prompt: Name the farther stand and the isolation. 85mm portrait of [Subject], compressed background, rapid falloff, isolation, the face as the only country.
items.definition: An 85mm portrait in 85mm cinematography is a short telephoto used from a farther stand so a head-and-shoulders stays large while the background enlarges and recedes in importance. The person becomes the landscape; the room becomes stacked color and shape behind them.

items.name: 135mm Telephoto
items.prompt: Name the distant stand and the crowded background. 135mm telephoto on [Subject], stacked planes, eavesdropping compression, background crowding the figure.
items.definition: A 135mm telephoto in 135mm cinematography is a long lens used from a distant stand so planes stack and the background crowds the figure. The image feels like eavesdropping: you are far away, yet the world presses in.

items.name: 200mm Long Telephoto
items.prompt: Name the extreme throw and the air. 200mm long lens on [Subject], extreme compression, heat shimmer, isolated from a distance, sniper intimacy.
items.definition: A 200mm long telephoto in 200mm cinematography is an extreme long lens used from a very distant stand so size differences between planes almost vanish. Heat shimmer, stacked terrain, and sniper intimacy are the physical leftovers of that throw.

items.name: Anamorphic
items.prompt: Name the squeeze and the artifacts you actually want. Anamorphic 2x on [Subject], oval bokeh, horizontal flares, widescreen squeeze character.
items.definition: Anamorphic cinematography squeezes one image dimension during capture, usually horizontally by 2x, then expands it for presentation. Depending on the lens, that cylindrical squeeze can produce oval bokeh, directional flares, and distinctive edge behavior; a wide aspect ratio alone is not anamorphic photography.

items.name: Spherical
items.prompt: Name the lack of squeeze. Spherical prime on [Subject], round bokeh, rectilinear edges, clean modern capture, no anamorphic streak.
items.definition: A spherical lens in spherical lens cinematography uses rotationally symmetric elements with no anamorphic squeeze, so the image is captured already in its display proportions. Bokeh from a round iris is round, and edges stay rectilinear aside from ordinary wide-angle stretch.

items.name: Fisheye
items.prompt: Name the projection. Fisheye on [Subject], circular or extreme barrel distortion, a world wrapping around a face, subjective unreality.
items.definition: A fisheye in fisheye cinematography is a very wide curvilinear projection that bends straight lines, especially away from the center. The world wraps around the lens; architecture becomes a bowl rather than a rectilinear box.

items.name: Tilt-Shift
items.prompt: Name real scale, then the thin focus plane. A real-scale city or citadel with [Subject] human-sized.
items.definition: Tilt-shift cinematography tilts the lens relative to the sensor so the plane of focus rotates, and may also shift the lens to slide perspective. A narrow band or shaped region of sharpness, often from a high viewpoint, can make a real-scale scene resemble a small model.

items.name: Macro
items.prompt: Name the optic and the centimeter. Macro lens on a detail of [Subject], insects of texture, an eye, a watch, a drop of rain, a world in a centimeter.
items.definition: Macro cinematography is close-focusing optics that let a small object or surface occupy the image at high reproduction scale, often near 1:1. An unusually close view turns texture, insects, eyes, or mechanisms into the entire shot.

items.name: Probe Lens
items.prompt: Name the tube and the interior path. Probe-lens view of [Subject], tiny wide lens on a stick, impossible proximity through glass, food, or machinery, miniature world.
items.definition: A probe lens is a long, narrow macro optic that can pass through small spaces and create extreme close moving shots from inside the subject. The front element is tiny and far from the camera body, so the viewpoint can enter a glass, a wound of machinery, food, or a miniature set.

items.name: Split Diopter
items.prompt: Name one room and two sharp zones. One continuous room: a near object on the left tack-sharp and [Subject] far on the right also tack-sharp, a narrow blur band between them.
items.definition: A split diopter is a partial close-focus element that keeps different distance zones sharp in one frame. One region focuses very near while another remains focused farther away; it is not two focal lengths, and it is not ordinary deep focus.

items.name: Vintage Cine Glass
items.prompt: Name the glass, not a sticker. Vintage cine glass on [Subject], lower contrast, gentle halation, swirling edges, Cooke or K35 character, not clinical sharpness.
items.definition: Vintage cine glass is older motion-picture optics whose coatings, contrast, and aberrations differ from modern clinical primes. Lower contrast, gentle halation, and sometimes swirling or rolling edges are properties of the lens, not a grade slapped on sharp digital.

items.name: Telephoto Compression
items.prompt: Name the collapsed distances, not only the lens. Telephoto compression stacking [Subject] against a wall of background, distances collapsed, crowded air, no escape in depth.
items.definition: Telephoto compression in lens compression cinematography is the perspective effect of a distant viewpoint: size differences between separated depth planes shrink, so a crowd or a city appears to press against a person. A long lens then frames that distant view tightly; a long lens from a close stand does not create the effect.

items.name: Magnification
items.prompt: Name the lost scale. Extreme magnification of [Subject], a world inside a centimeter, scale lost on purpose.
items.definition: Magnification in magnification cinematography is the ratio of the subject's image size on the sensor to its real size. High magnification makes a centimeter of the world fill the frame; it is a scale number, not a shot-size name and not automatically a macro lens.

items.name: Teal and Orange
items.prompt: Protect skin, then split the rest. Teal-and-orange grade on [Subject], skin staying warm, shadows and skies pushed cyan, complementary split.
items.definition: A teal and orange color grade pushes shadows and often skies toward cyan-teal while keeping skin and warm sources in the orange half of the wheel. It is a complementary split with faces protected, not a silver-retention process and not a general cool wash.

items.name: Bleach Bypass
items.prompt: Name silver, crush, and metal. Bleach-bypass look on [Subject], retained silver, crushed color, harsh contrast, metallic midtones.
items.definition: Bleach bypass retains silver during processing, or simulates that retention, so the dye image sits on leftover metallic density. Contrast rises, grain shows, saturation falls, and highlights turn harsh rather than candy-colored.

items.name: Monochrome
items.prompt: Ban hue explicitly. Monochrome treatment of [Subject], silver highlights, deep blacks, no chroma, shape and light only.
items.definition: Monochrome, including black and white cinematography, removes or does not record chromatic information so the image is value, texture, and shape. Hue is gone; contrast, grain, and outline do the talking.

items.name: Sepia
items.prompt: Map the scale to brown-gold. Sepia tonality on [Subject], brown-gold memory, faded whites, the past as a color, not a filter sticker.
items.definition: Sepia tone in sepia tone film maps the grey scale onto brown-gold instead of neutral silver, so whites go toward faded paper and blacks toward umber. It is a color of the past as chemistry, not a warm grade on a full-hue world.

items.name: Desaturation
items.prompt: Pull chroma, keep accents. Desaturated palette on [Subject], chroma pulled back, dusty, wintered, emotion in leftover color accents.
items.definition: Desaturation in desaturated cinematography reduces color intensity while leaving hue present. The world is wintered or dusted; leftover accents still speak, but chroma is no longer loud.

items.name: Hyper-Saturation
items.prompt: Name intensity, not a mood word. Hyper-saturated color on [Subject], Velvia intensity, reds like lacquer, a dream or a fever, not documentary.
items.definition: Hyper-saturation in saturated cinematography raises color intensity past ordinary record, so hues read as lacquer, fever, or dream. Feeling is louder than fact; the palette is not documentary.

items.name: Cool Blue
items.prompt: Name the steel and the reserved hearth. Cool blue grade on [Subject], steel shadows, hospital or moonlight, warmth reserved for one practical if any.
items.definition: A cool blue grade in cool color grade work shifts the image toward steel, cyan, or moonlight blues across shadows and often midtones. Warmth, if it survives, is reserved for a practical or a face that the story wants to save.

items.name: Warm Amber
items.prompt: Name honey mids and practical glow. Warm amber grade on [Subject], tungsten honey, candle and practical glow, safety or nostalgia in the mids.
items.definition: A warm amber grade in warm color grade work biases mids and highlights toward tungsten honey, candle, and practical glow. Safety, home, or nostalgia sits in the mids; the world is invited rather than chilled.

items.name: Filmic Faded
items.prompt: Name the print curve. Filmic faded grade on [Subject], lifted blacks, rolled-off highlights, print-emulation, slightly expired romance.
items.definition: A filmic faded grade in filmic color grade work imitates a print: blacks are lifted off true zero, highlights roll off instead of clipping like video, and contrast sits like photochemical display. It is not HDR punch, and it is not automatically period costume.

items.name: Cross Process
items.prompt: Name the wrong primaries. Cross-processed look on [Subject], skewed primaries, cyan shadows, magenta skin shift, music-video chemical accident.
items.definition: A cross process look imitates developing a film in the wrong chemistry, such as slide stock in color-negative developer, so primaries skew off their true identities. Contrast often climbs; cyan shadows, magenta or yellow skin shifts, and other chemical accidents become the palette.

items.name: Day for Night
items.prompt: Hide the day, keep the land. Day-for-night treatment of [Subject], underexposed daylight, blue wash, skipped-over sun, moonlight as a lie that reads.
items.definition: Day for night cinematography photographs daylight so it will read as nighttime while still showing terrain that true night might hide. Exposure, sky, and highlight control do the lying; a blue wash alone is not the technique.

items.name: Tungsten Balance
items.prompt: Name 3200K and the cold window. Tungsten-balanced interior on [Subject], 3200K warmth, windows going cold blue, mixed sources telling inside versus out.
items.definition: Tungsten balance in tungsten color temperature work sets the camera or stock for about 3200K so tungsten practicals render near-neutral or gently warm while daylight and cooler sources go blue. Different source colors remain visibly distinct rather than being normalized to one white.

items.name: Moonlight Gel
items.prompt: Name the cool key and the underexposure. Moonlight gel on [Subject], cyan-green night, a single cool key as the moon, deep underexposure, silver edges.
items.definition: Moonlight gel in moonlight lighting gel work is a cool, often cyan or steel-green key standing in for the moon, usually a large source from above or through trees. Night stays sculpted: there is a direction, a rim, and deep underexposure, not only a blue grade.

items.name: Split Toning
items.prompt: Name both hues and which owns shadows. Split-toned grade on [Subject], highlights one hue, shadows another, for example gold over teal, a two-color world.
items.definition: Split toning in split toning cinematography assigns one hue to highlights and another to shadows, so the tone curve becomes a two-color world. Any pair is legal; teal-and-orange is only one famous instance.

items.name: Natural Grade
items.prompt: Forbid the splits by name. Natural grade on [Subject], faithful skin, restrained saturation, no stylized split, the location's real color science.
items.definition: A natural color grade keeps skin faithful and saturation restrained so the location's real color science remains the authority. No stylized split, no silver punishment, no fever: the grade mostly refuses to editorialize hue.

items.name: Color Shift
items.prompt: Name the before and after. Color shift across [Subject], hues sliding mid-shot or mid-grade, a world that changes temperature in front of us.
items.definition: A color shift effect is a change of color state that the audience is meant to notice: monochrome to hue, one world to another, or a slide of temperature during the shot. Color is the event, not a hidden LUT.

items.name: Vintage
items.prompt: Name dyes and bloom, not stickers. Vintage treatment of [Subject], faded dyes, halation, the past as chemistry, not a sticker.
items.definition: A vintage film look treats the image as past chemistry: faded dyes, possible halation, softened contrast, and period color that has drifted. It is a whole-file costume of time, not only old glass and not only a lifted print curve.

items.name: Palette
items.prompt: Name the allowed hues and ban the rest. Restricted palette on [Subject], a few chosen hues doing all the work, design as law.
items.definition: A color palette in color palette cinematography is a restricted set of hues used as law across set, costume, light, and grade. Too many colors would be noise; a few chosen hues do all the work and can mark location, timeline, or story state.

items.name: Overexposed
items.prompt: Name the burn. Overexposed [Subject], values clipping toward heaven or fluorescent hell, information burned on purpose.
items.definition: Overexposed cinematography lets values clip or bloom toward white on purpose so information in the highlights is burned. It is a choice to lose the top of the scale, not the same as high-key lighting, which can stay bright while still holding detail.

items.name: Slow Motion
items.prompt: Name the fps feel and what the extra time reveals. Still: a physically plausible mid-action pose with hanging dust, delayed fabric, and readable contacts, not a statue.
items.definition: Slow motion cinematography plays action over more screen time than the event occupied during capture, usually by overcranking (recording 120 to 240 fps and playing at 24). The extra samples reveal fabric delay, particle hang, and impact mechanics that a 24 fps shutter would compress into a few smeared frames.

items.name: Fast Motion
items.prompt: State that time is compressed and what races. Still: a pose that implies acceleration (smeared extras, streaked traffic) while the subject, if they must stay readable, holds.
items.definition: Fast motion cinematography compresses screen duration so action plays faster than it occurred, by undercranking the camera or by retiming a normal-rate take. Crowds smear, clouds race, and labor can look absurdly efficient because too many events occupy too little time.

items.name: Speed Ramp
items.prompt: Name the real-time approach, the stretched beat, and the recovery. Still: three readable phases implied in one pose is weaker than a video ramp.
items.definition: Speed ramping changes playback or capture speed inside a single shot rather than holding one retiming ratio. Approach and recovery stay energetic while one motivated instant (impact, glance, turn) stretches, then the clock returns.

items.name: Freeze Frame
items.prompt: Write a hold, not a slow pose. Still: the chosen frame as a photograph with grain, a decisive expression or body shape, no implied smear.
items.definition: A freeze frame holds one image so narrative time stops while camera, subject, and world all cease to generate new samples. The hold can end a story, land a joke, or present a face as evidence.

items.name: Time-Lapse
items.prompt: Name the interval collapse and what must move. Still: matched architecture at one implied phase, or a composite of sun angles only if you label it a study.
items.definition: Time-lapse cinematography captures frames at long intervals so slow change plays as continuous motion, hours becoming seconds as shadows sweep and crowds become flow. It is interval photography, not a sped-up ordinary take.

items.name: Step Printing
items.prompt: Ask for duplicated frames and in-frame smear, not 120 fps. Still: a readable figure with strongly smeared passersby, long-exposure street texture.
items.definition: Step printing repeats or omits frames optically or digitally so motion advances in visible temporal steps. Combined with low-rate capture and long exposures, each frame smears internally while the sequence stutters forward, a texture of delay rather than clean high-frame-rate slow motion.

items.name: Reverse Motion
items.prompt: Name inverted physics, not a shuffled outline. Still: a tell such as rain hanging upward, glass mid-reassembly, smoke drawing in.
items.definition: Reverse motion plays recorded action backward so causes arrive after their effects inside the shot: rain rises, smoke inhales, a shattered object reassembles. This is reversed playback, not a story told in reverse scene order.

items.name: Bullet Time
items.prompt: Write two clocks: action stopped or crushed, camera continuing on a path. Still: one instant seen as if from a step along an orbit, hanging debris, consistent anatomy.
items.definition: Bullet time freezes or radically slows action while the viewpoint travels around it, decoupling camera speed from subject time. The instant becomes inspectable space: a time-slice orbit around a sculpture of speed, not ordinary slow motion with a handheld camera.

items.name: Long Take
items.prompt: Write unbroken duration and what happens in depth. Still: a wide ensemble with a readable route, not proof of a take.
items.definition: Long take cinematography is an unusually extended shot that preserves continuous performance, space, action, or duration without an overt cut. Blocking and camera share one sentence so the audience cannot leave the room.

items.name: Oner
items.prompt: Write a whole scene as one take. Still: a frame from the path, not proof.
items.definition: A oner shot is designed to play as if the scene were one take, with no visible edits. It may be a true single take or a stitched oner whose joins hide in whips, darkness, or crossing bodies.

items.name: Motion Blur
items.prompt: Commit to streaks. Still: lamps as ribbons, bodies smearing, a subject sharp only if they held still.
items.definition: Motion blur cinematography is the streaking or softness caused by subject or camera movement during exposure. The longer the gate stays open relative to the motion, the more the image paints, so edges fail on purpose.

items.name: Stutter / Stop-Stutter
items.prompt: Write frames dropping or repeating, not smear and not a jump in angle. Still: a face or gesture that looks temporally sampled, slight after-images only if they come from repeats.
items.definition: Stutter editing drops or repeats frames so playback skips and the world's clock hitches. It is an anxious rhythm, not the lyric smear of step printing and not a jump cut's spatial jump.

items.name: Boomerang
items.prompt: Write the round trip. Still: the mid-gesture peak, because a still cannot boomerang.
items.definition: A boomerang video effect plays a short action forward, then snaps it backward along the same samples, often looping. The gesture comes and goes on one path: reversed playback used as a round trip rather than a one-way undo.

items.name: Infinite Loop
items.prompt: Say whether you want a seamless visual sew or a repeated-day story. Still: a pose that could be both start and end.
items.definition: An infinite loop video sews the last frame to the first so motion never arrives at an ending. The cycle can be a seamless visual join, or, in narrative use, a repeated day whose variables change.

items.name: Stop Motion
items.prompt: Write materials and increments, not a filter. Still: a puppet or object mid-pose, visible construction, coherent joints.
items.definition: Stop motion cinematography photographs physical objects incrementally, adjusting them between exposures so successive poses create apparent movement. The cadence is pose to pose and slightly staccato, with tactile materials in the light.

items.name: Low Shutter
items.prompt: Adapt the catalog line toward the physics: short shutter, not long smear. Still: crisp droplets and defined moving limbs in a tense handheld frame.
items.definition: Low shutter cinematography uses a short shutter angle or short exposure so moving edges stay sharp inside each frame. Normal-rate action then feels abrupt and staccato because this is reduced motion blur, not a long-exposure smear.

items.name: Timelapse Glam
items.prompt: Lock the face, accelerate the styling. Still: one held identity with evidence of process (hands, garments in mid-swap).
items.definition: Timelapse glam is interval photography of a styling process in which clothes, hair, and makeup change at high speed while the face holds. The person is a still axis and wardrobe is the changing weather.

items.name: Timelapse Human
items.prompt: Hold the person, lapse the crowd. Still: one sharp figure, pedestrians as flow, stable sun unless you want a day.
items.definition: Timelapse human holds one person in living time while the crowd is interval-sampled into smoke, so one still will stands in a rushing system. It is the opposite clock of a frozen world with a moving hero.

items.name: Timelapse Landscape
items.prompt: Write light and weather as the motion. Still: one honest sun angle on stable geology.
items.definition: Timelapse landscape interval-samples light and weather over a place so hours play in seconds as clouds and shadows sweep. Geography is the actor, and a person, if present, is a scale mark rather than a racing extra.

items.name: Frozen in Motion
items.prompt: Name who moves. Still: one active subject in a square of frozen pedestrians and hanging debris.
items.definition: Frozen in motion stops the environment and most people while a chosen character, the viewpoint, or both continue to move. Particles, extras, and pigeons hang, and the rule of who may move is the entire effect.

items.name: Moonwalk
items.prompt: Write the slide, not a reverse clip. Still: mid-glide, one foot flat, torso upright, coat trailing.
items.definition: A moonwalk effect is a backward glide that reads as a forward myth: the torso stays upright, one foot slides, the other pushes, and the heel does not lift like a walk. It is a locomotion lie in living time, not reversed footage.

items.name: Lens Flare
items.prompt: Name the source and the glass, not a pack. Example: Lens flare across [Subject], the sun or a hard practical striking the front element, veiling contrast, ghost orbs tracking the source, source-linked not floating.
items.definition: Lens flare in lens flare cinematography is stray light scattered by glass, coatings, and barrel walls, producing ghosts, streaks, or veiling glare instead of a clean image. The artifacts live in the taking optic, so they track the source angle and dim when a body occludes the lamp.

items.name: Anamorphic Flare
items.prompt: State squeeze and streak axis. Example: Horizontal anamorphic flares streaking through [Subject], cyan or magenta bars from headlights or neon, oval bokeh, 2x squeeze, not round spherical ghosts.
items.definition: An anamorphic flare is a horizontal streak produced when a bright point hits the cylindrical elements of an anamorphic lens. It is a subset of lens flare, not a general haze, and it usually arrives with oval bokeh from the same squeeze.

items.name: Halation
items.prompt: Bloom the highlight edge, not the whole room. Example: Halation glow around highlights on [Subject], red-edge bloom of film stock, lamps breathing, eyes and fabric texture preserved, not a global fog.
items.definition: Halation in film is a reddish or warm glow around bright highlights caused by light passing through the emulsion, reflecting off the base, and scattering back into the image. It is a stock behavior, not a diffusion filter and not flare inside the lens.

items.name: Film Grain
items.prompt: Specify format and that the grain is in the image, not on it. Example: Visible film grain over [Subject], 35mm or 16mm dye-cloud texture, temporally unstable, denser in shadows, not a cheap overlay.
items.definition: Film grain in film grain cinematography is the random texture of silver halide crystals or color dye clouds in the emulsion, or a digital simulation of that structure. It is a developed surface, not a PNG overlay sitting on top of a clean render.

items.name: Bokeh
items.prompt: Name disc shape and highlight sources. Example: Creamy bokeh field behind [Subject], circular or oval highlight discs from practicals, subject sharp, background as light not as a masked blur.
items.definition: Bokeh in bokeh cinematography is the aesthetic character of out-of-focus rendering: the disc shape, edge, and smoothness of blurred points, not the mere fact of a thin depth of field. The glass, not a blur slider, decides whether those discs are round, oval, outlined, or swirling.

items.name: Double Exposure
items.prompt: Name both records and the mix. Example: Double exposure of [Subject] overlaid with a second named image, faces in cities, a ghost in rain, optical composite in camera, both exposures visible, not a morph and not a split-screen join.
items.definition: Double exposure in double exposure film combines two or more image records on one frame, in camera by winding back, optically in a printer, or digitally as an additive composite. Both pictures occupy the same emulsion or file unless a matte fully holds one off.

items.name: Rack Focus
items.prompt: Name both planes and the duration. Still: Rack focus between planes around [Subject], a two-second pull from foreground to the figure or the reverse.
items.definition: A rack focus moves the sharp plane from one subject or distance to another during a continuous shot, while the composition stays largely the same. Attention changes because the helical turns, not because the camera cuts or dollies.

items.name: Shallow Focus
items.prompt: Name the mark and the stop. Example: Very shallow focus on [Subject], T1.4, near eye sharp, background dissolved into optical discs, intimacy by exclusion, not a cutout mask.
items.definition: Shallow focus keeps a narrow depth range sharp while foreground or background falls off. It is a depth-of-field choice made with distance, focal length, and aperture together, not a button labeled blur.

items.name: Deep Focus
items.prompt: Demand continuous sharpness, not two cut planes. Example: Deep focus on [Subject] and the far plane, near action and distant doorway both sharp, no rack focus, no split-diopter seam, the eye may wander.
items.definition: Deep focus in deep focus cinematography keeps multiple near and far planes legibly sharp in one image. It is a continuous depth of field, not merely action arranged in depth while the glass stays selective.

items.name: Forced Perspective
items.prompt: Describe the viewpoint lie, not a shrink filter. Example: Forced perspective with [Subject], scale altered by camera placement and scaled furniture, giant or miniature in camera, locked viewpoint, matching eyelines, not a digital resize.
items.definition: Forced perspective uses camera position, subject distance, and set geometry to alter apparent size or distance, and the lie exists only from the taking viewpoint. Bodies, furniture, and eyelines must agree or the scale collapses.

items.name: Light Leak
items.prompt: Put the wound on the edge, not on the sun. Example: Analog light leak washing [Subject], orange or red fog eating the frame edge, unfiltered light on the emulsion, not a source-linked lens flare.
items.definition: A light leak in light leak film is unfiltered light that reaches the emulsion or sensor without passing through the taking lens, usually through a gap in the body, magazine, or gate. It fogs from the edge or along a scratch in the film path, often orange or red on color negative because it hits the base side.

items.name: Vignette
items.prompt: Ask for lens falloff, not a baked oval. Example: Natural optical vignette around [Subject], corners a stop down, attention pooled in the center, vintage falloff not a post oval.
items.definition: A vignette in vignette cinematography darkens, desaturates, or lowers contrast toward the frame edges because of optical falloff, mechanical vignetting in the barrel, a filter, or a later grade. Optical vignette follows the lens, while a post oval is a drawing.

items.name: Chromatic Aberration
items.prompt: Fringe the edges, do not split the body. Example: Chromatic aberration on [Subject], red-cyan fringing at high-contrast edges, stronger toward the corners, vintage or simple glass, not a full RGB channel offset.
items.definition: Chromatic aberration in chromatic aberration cinematography is color fringing from different wavelengths focusing at different distances or magnifications. Lateral CA puts red-cyan (or similar) fringes on high-contrast edges, worse toward the frame edge, while longitudinal CA puts different colors in front of and behind the focus plane.

items.name: Infrared
items.prompt: Specify near-IR reflectance, not heat. Example: Infrared look on [Subject], foliage going pale, skies black, skin waxy, near-infrared photograph, not night-vision green, not a thermal palette.
items.definition: Infrared cinematography photographs near-infrared reflectance (roughly 700 to 900 nm), not heat, so foliage often goes pale, skies go dark, and skin can look waxy. It is a different slice of reflected light, still a photograph of the location.

items.name: Night Vision
items.prompt: Make it a device, not a grade. Example: Night-vision green phosphor of [Subject], grainy image intensification, blooming lamps, goggle or sight framing, surveillance or military eye, not a thermal palette.
items.definition: Night vision in night vision cinematography is image intensification: residual photons, and often a near-IR illuminator, amplified through a photocathode and microchannel plate onto a phosphor. The picture is typically green, grainy, blooming around lamps, with the framing of goggles, a weapon sight, or a camera in the dark.

items.name: Thermal
items.prompt: Map temperature, not lamps. Example: Thermal palette of [Subject], heat as color, faces as warm masks, ironbow or white-hot, search-and-rescue or predator vision, not night-vision green, not pale infrared foliage.
items.definition: Thermal imaging cinematography maps emitted long-wave infrared (heat), not reflected light. A microbolometer or similar sensor assigns a palette (white-hot, black-hot, ironbow) to temperature, so faces, engines, and blood read warm while cold metal and night air do not.

items.name: Slit-Scan
items.prompt: Ask for ordered temporal geometry. Example: Slit-scan streaking around [Subject], time smeared along one axis, structured corridor of light with a stable vanishing point, Star Gate language, no random neon particles.
items.definition: Slit-scan exposes moving artwork or a moving camera through a narrow slit over time, stretching space into streaks and corridors with time laid along one axis. The result is structured geometry, not a random particle tunnel.

items.name: Kaleidoscope
items.prompt: Demand mirrors or radial shards. Example: Kaleidoscopic fragmentation of [Subject], mirrored shards, radial symmetry, Busby Berkeley from inside a jewel, not a slit-scan tunnel.
items.definition: Kaleidoscope cinematography fragments the image with mirrors or radial repetition so one subject becomes a symmetric pattern. The camera looks into angled glass, or the staging itself is a kaleidoscope: bodies arranged around an axis, often from above.

items.name: Light Flash
items.prompt: Make it an event with a recovery. Still: Blinding light flash over [Subject], a bulb, explosion, or memory cut, the frame going to white then returning.
items.definition: A light flash transition is a brief blowout of the frame to white or near-white, then a return, as if a bulb, explosion, or memory dump hit the emulsion. It is a temporal event, often a cut hidden in the peak, not a standing lens flare.

items.name: Projections
items.prompt: Put the image on a surface. Example: Projected imagery crawling over [Subject] and architecture, a plate on a screen or faces on walls, foreground lit to match the projection, in-camera process not a double-exposure ghost.
items.definition: Projections in projection mapping film put a pictured image onto a surface that the taking camera then photographs: front projection onto a retroreflective screen, rear projection behind a window or windshield, or video mapped onto architecture. The projector is a light source, and the set is also a screen.

items.name: Morph
items.prompt: Name both states and the duration. Still: Morph between [Subject] and another named state, face or body becoming, in-between geometry visible.
items.definition: A morphing effect transforms one image, face, shape, or object into another by interpolating corresponding geometry over time. It is a continuous becoming, not a crossfade of opacities and not two exposures stacked.

items.name: Altered State
items.prompt: List the perceptual tells. Still: Altered-state image of [Subject], smear, afterimage, wrong color, time that will not sit still.
items.definition: Altered state cinematography makes the mind the location: smear, afterimage, wrong color, unstable time, optics and cutting that no sober observer would report. It is a bundle of techniques motivated by consciousness, not a single filter name.

items.name: Anthropo
items.prompt: Cover the thing like a person. Example: Anthropomorphic frame of [Subject], an object or animal given human scale, gesture, or eyeline, singles and looks as if it had a will, not a camera inside the object.
items.definition: Anthropomorphic cinematography stages an object or animal as a performer: human scale in the frame, a gesture, an eyeline, reaction shots, as if the inanimate had a will. The camera does not need a face so much as an actor's grammar.

items.name: Cinemagraph
items.prompt: Freeze the frame, license one cycle. Still: Cinemagraph of [Subject], almost a still, one isolated motion looping: steam, hair, a blink, rain in a window.
items.definition: A cinemagraph is a still photograph in which one isolated element continues to move on a loop (steam, rain on glass, hair, a blink) while the rest of the frame is frozen. It is not a freeze-frame of a whole shot, and it is not a full clip that happens to loop.

items.name: Collage
items.prompt: Show the joins. Example: Collage frame of [Subject], torn layers, mixed stocks, cut paper and live action sharing one plane, visible edges, not a smooth optical overlay.
items.definition: Collage cinematography builds a frame from torn, cut, or mixed pieces: different stocks, paper, print, and live action sharing one plane with visible joins. Edges are graphic, and the stack is a construction, not an optical blend.

items.name: Datamosh
items.prompt: Break prediction, not the lens. Still: Datamosh of [Subject], inter-frame collapse, faces smearing into the next GOP, digital ruin as style.
items.definition: Datamosh is intentional codec failure: inter-frame prediction continues after keyframes are removed or broken, so motion vectors smear the previous picture into the next GOP and faces bleed into the following shot. The image is file wreckage, not a lens error.

items.name: Diorama
items.prompt: Photograph a model as a world. Example: Diorama view of [Subject], physical miniature, tactile surfaces, deep enough focus for full-size scale, slow camera, not tilt-shift toy blur.
items.definition: Diorama cinematography photographs a physical scale model so that it stands in for a much larger object or environment, with real light hitting real miniature surfaces. Scale is sold by texture, camera speed, depth of field, and movement, not by a toy-like tilt of focus.

items.name: Distortions
items.prompt: Bend the space with glass. Example: Optical distortion around [Subject], stretched edges, barrel or melted geometry from ultra-wide or fisheye glass close to the face, the lens lying about space, not a flare pack.
items.definition: Lens distortion cinematography warps space so straight lines bow, stretch, or melt: barrel, pincushion, mustache, extreme wide stretch, or a physical distorting optic such as a diopter, a bottle, or rain on glass. The lens is lying about geometry, not adding flare.

items.name: Duplication
items.prompt: Two solid performances, one space. Example: Duplication of [Subject], the same figure twice in one frame, twins of identity, solid bodies with matched light and contact shadows, not a double-exposure ghost, not a visible split-screen line.
items.definition: A duplicate subject effect puts the same performer in a frame more than once as solid bodies: twins, a self across a table, copies in one room. It is usually a split matte, motion control, or a locked-camera composite, not a translucent double exposure.

items.name: Echo Print
items.prompt: Write the still as a photochemical hold, then name the ghost. Quote: Echo print of [Subject], a ghosted afterimage offset in time or register, the last frame still printed on this one.
items.definition: An echo print is an echo print effect that leaves a ghosted afterimage offset in time or register, so the last pose is still printed on this frame. The ghost is a stain of a previous exposure, not a second complete picture sharing the same plane.

items.name: Feedback
items.prompt: Video feedback around [Subject], camera looking into its own output, infinite corridor of the same face. For video: Recursive video feedback of [Subject], the image eating itself into a tunnel.
items.definition: Video feedback is made by pointing a camera at its own live output so the picture nests into a recursive corridor of the same face. Each generation is a rephotograph of the monitor, with bloom, lag, and a tunnel of shrinking frames.

items.name: Floating UI
items.prompt: Floating UI over [Subject], HUD, callouts, and interface planes in 3D space, the screen as a cockpit. Name what the panels say in plain language, keep type sharp, and say the planes parallax if the camera moves.
items.definition: Floating UI, or HUD overlay cinematography, places readable interface, callouts, and data planes in the air of the scene so information lives in space, not only on a physical screen. The cockpit is the room.

items.name: Focal Shift
items.prompt: Focal shift on [Subject], the plane of sharpness traveling from one fact to another, attention as a pull. Video: Focus pulls from a foreground object onto [Subject], or the reverse.
items.definition: A focal shift moves the plane of sharpness from one subject or distance to another during the shot, so attention travels as a pull. The camera body can stay put, and only the focus mechanism walks the depth.

items.name: Generative
items.prompt: Generative image of [Subject], forms grown by rule, particles, and iteration, cinema made by a system. Name the rule and the light on the bits.
items.definition: Generative visuals show process: forms grown by rule, particles, and iteration, so cinema is made by a system rather than only by a finished photograph. Making is visible.

items.name: Levitation
items.prompt: Levitation of [Subject], body or object refusing gravity, a quiet impossible hover. Video: [Subject] hangs in air, slow drift, no visible support.
items.definition: A levitation shot holds a body or object in a quiet impossible hover, refusing ordinary gravity while support is hidden or removed. Hair and cloth still hang, and the gap under the feet is the proof.

items.name: Masking
items.prompt: Masked frame around [Subject], a shape cutting the picture, binoculars, a keyhole, a graphic window. Name the shape, keep the interior photographed, and keep the surround opaque.
items.definition: Masking cinematography uses a matte, a viewfinder object, or a graphic window so looking is visible as a shape cutting the picture. We see through binoculars, a keyhole, or a hard-edged hole.

items.name: Mixed Media
items.prompt: Mixed media around [Subject], live action, type, illustration, and stock colliding in one plane. Name each medium.
items.definition: Mixed media film combines live action with type, illustration, and stock in one plane so no single capture method owns the truth of the frame. Media collide rather than dissolve into one photograph.

items.name: Morphing
items.prompt: Morph of [Subject] into another state, continuous transformation, identity as a dissolve you can watch. Video: [Subject] morphs into another form over the shot.
items.definition: Morphing cinematography transforms one shape or image continuously into another by interpolating geometry, rather than merely fading between pictures. Identity is a dissolve you can watch as contour.

items.name: Object Portal
items.prompt: Object portal through [Subject], a thing opening onto another space, a bag, a screen, a doorway that should not lead there. Name the prop, the rim, and the far geography inside it.
items.definition: An object portal effect treats a prop as a wormhole: a bag, a screen, or a doorway that should not lead there, opening onto another space. The thing is the cut.

items.name: Photogrammetry
items.prompt: Photogrammetry look of [Subject], scanned space, slightly wrong mesh, a real place turned into a model. Name overlapping-photo texture, a hole or stretch, and an orbit or inspection camera.
items.definition: The photogrammetry look reconstructs 3D geometry and texture from overlapping photographs, so a real place is turned into a scanned mesh. Slightly wrong normals, stretched texture, and holes are the evidence of capture.

items.name: Ratio Switch
items.prompt: Aspect-ratio switch on [Subject], the frame itself widening or closing as the story changes register. Video: The frame around [Subject] changes aspect ratio during the sequence, a visible crop or reveal.
items.definition: An aspect ratio switch changes the image's visible boundaries so the container itself widens or closes as the story changes register. The picture is not stretched: previously unseen area is revealed, or the crop tightens.

items.name: Scale Shift
items.prompt: Scale shift of [Subject], the body suddenly giant or tiny against the same room, Alice physics. Name the room, the new size, and matching shadows.
items.definition: Scale shift cinematography changes a body's size against the same room so the figure is suddenly giant or tiny: Alice physics as an optical event. Furniture, shadows, and contact have to match the new ratio.

items.name: Shadow Box
items.prompt: Shadow-box of [Subject], layered cut-outs, depth as stacked silhouettes, a diorama of darkness. Name several planes, a hard backlight, and no fill on the figures.
items.definition: Shadow-box cinematography tells the story in layered cut-outs, depth as stacked silhouettes, a diorama of darkness. Figures are unfilled, and distance is paper stacked in front of a hard backlight.

items.name: Transformation
items.prompt: Transformation of [Subject], a body, room, or object becoming something else in continuous view. Video: [Subject] transforms across the shot, a visible change of state.
items.definition: Transformation cinematography makes a body, room, or object become something else in continuous view. The camera keeps watching while the state changes, with a stable anchor so the becoming can be read.

items.name: Typography
items.prompt: Typography in the world of [Subject], words as objects, titles that occupy space, kinetic type. Name the words, the surface they sit on, and the light.
items.definition: Kinetic typography puts words in the world of the shot as objects: titles that occupy space, letters with scale, parallax, and a surface. The sentence is in the picture, not parked as a caption.

items.name: Wigglegram
items.prompt: Wigglegram of [Subject], two or three frames rocking, a cheap stereo shiver, depth as a fidget. Video: A short wiggle between two viewpoints of [Subject], stereoscopic shiver.
items.definition: A wigglegram is a short stereo shiver: two or three frames rocking so depth reads as a fidget. The viewpoints are a few centimeters apart, so depth is a twitch, not a dolly.

items.name: X-Ray
items.prompt: X-ray view of [Subject], interior structure, bones or wiring, a body as diagram. Demand transmission, a readable skeleton or circuit, and no thermal palette.
items.definition: X-ray cinematography images through a surface as if denser structure were visible: bones, wiring, a body as diagram. Transmission, not reflectance, is the physics.

items.name: Zoetrope
items.prompt: Zoetrope of [Subject], stroboscopic slices of a spinning action, motion as a drum of frames. Video: Stroboscopic zoetrope slices of [Subject] in repeating action.
items.definition: Zoetrope cinematography shows the frames inside a movement: stroboscopic slices of a spinning action, motion as a drum of poses. You see the sampling, not a smooth blur.

items.name: Focus Change
items.prompt: Focus change on [Subject], the plane of sharpness jumping or sliding to a new fact, a rack without apology. Video: Focus changes from one plane onto [Subject] or away from them.
items.definition: Focus change cinematography jumps or slides the plane of sharpness to a new fact, a rack without apology. The mid-blur is short, and the new plane owns the shot as soon as it lands.

items.name: Floating Fall
items.prompt: Floating fall of [Subject], a body hanging in slow drop, weightless disaster, hair and coat in delayed gravity. Video: [Subject] falls in slow, floating pieces, delayed gravity, a dream of dropping.
items.definition: A floating fall is a body hanging in a slow drop: delayed gravity on hair and coat, still going down. The path remains toward the ground, even when the clock on the body is late.

items.name: Smash and Grab
items.prompt: Smash-and-grab energy on [Subject], glass, impact, snatch, handheld chaos, a theft of a moment. Video: Violent handheld smash around [Subject], impact, grab, escape.
items.definition: Smash-and-grab video is impact as coverage: glass, snatch, handheld chaos, a theft of a moment. The camera is inside the crime, too close and too late.

items.name: Cyclope
items.prompt: Cyclope view of [Subject], a single giant iris, fisheye as a monster eye, one hole looking. Demand barrel distortion, a catchlight, and a circular hole.
items.definition: A cyclope camera is one giant iris looking: fisheye as a monster eye, a single hole, too close. The lens is the creature.

items.name: Particles
items.prompt: Particles around [Subject], dust, sparks, pollen, a weather of bits, light catching each one. Name the species, a backlight, and that the bits are discrete.
items.definition: Particle effects cinematography fills the air with countable bits: dust, sparks, pollen, a weather of motes, each one catching light. Atmosphere you can inventory, not a blanket of fog.

items.name: Argus
items.prompt: Argus image of [Subject], many eyes, many viewpoints, a creature or a city of looking. Count the eyes.
items.definition: An Argus image, argus many eyes, fills the frame with looking: extra pupils on a body, a swarm of viewpoints, a creature or a city of eyes. The surplus is seeing, counted as organs or cameras, not as flare.

items.name: Sticker Peel
items.prompt: Sticker peel on [Subject], the image lifting from a backing, adhesive shine, a graphic coming off the world. Video: A sticker layer peels off [Subject] or the frame, revealing another layer.
items.definition: A sticker peel effect lifts the image from a backing: adhesive shine, a die-cut layer coming off the world. Thickness, curl, and glue are the physics, not a still collage of torn paper.

items.name: Selfie Twin
items.prompt: Selfie twin of [Subject], two of the same face in a phone-arm frame, identity as a double take. Demand the same person twice, compact-camera distortion, and a phone-arm wide.
items.definition: A selfie twin puts two of the same face in a phone-arm frame, identity as a double take at arm's length. The camera is a compact wide in a hand, not a hidden studio body.

items.name: Bubbles
items.prompt: Bubbles around [Subject], refraction worlds that still read as joy or threat. Demand soap-film surfaces, rainbow edges, and a repeated face in the spheres.
items.definition: Bubbles cinematography fills the air with little lenses: soap films that refract the subject, rainbow edges, wet highlights. Each bubble is an optic, not a disk of bokeh.

items.name: Match Cut
items.prompt: Write both sides of the join. Example: Match cut from [Subject] to a rhyming shape or motion in another time, graphic continuity across a hard cut, bone to station.
items.definition: A match cut joins two shots through a visual, spatial, sonic, or conceptual correspondence the viewer can read at the splice. The outgoing frame and the incoming frame share a shape, motion, object class, or idea, so the cut argues a relationship instead of only changing the view.

items.name: Graphic Match
items.prompt: Graphic match on the silhouette of [Subject], shape echoing shape, circle to circle, a visual rhyme. Specify the shared contour, its screen position, and that the objects stay distinct.
items.definition: A graphic match cut joins two images that share a dominant shape, line, color, placement, or motion pattern, even when location and time change. The outgoing contour and the incoming contour occupy the same part of the screen, so form carries you across the splice.

items.name: Match on Action
items.prompt: Match on action through [Subject]'s gesture, the motion started in one shot and finished in the next. Name the wide and the close, the hand, the object, the direction of travel, and that the cut happens during the move.
items.definition: Match on action cuts during one continuous action so the movement itself bridges two camera positions. The outgoing shot starts the gesture; the incoming shot finishes it, which is why the edit can change size or angle without feeling interrupted.

items.name: Jump Cut
items.prompt: Jump cut on [Subject], time skipped inside a similar framing, interruption, anxiety or comedy of missing frames. Specify a locked or near-locked setup, what changes (posture, clock, crowd), and that the camera does not morph.
items.definition: A jump cut removes time or slightly shifts framing inside a similar setup, so the discontinuity is conspicuous. The outgoing frame and the incoming frame are close enough that the missing interval reads as a skip, not as a new shot.

items.name: Smash Cut
items.prompt: Smash cut from [Subject] to a violently different image, silence to noise, prayer to explosion, no polite dissolve. Name the outgoing state (quiet, dark, small, resolved) and the incoming opposite (loud, bright, huge, ruptured).
items.definition: A smash cut makes an abrupt, high-contrast transition in image, sound, tone, scale, or time. The outgoing side has earned a state (quiet, prayer, resolution); the incoming side contradicts it without a polite blend.

items.name: Dissolve
items.prompt: Dissolve from [Subject] into another time or place, overlapping ghosts, a longer time than a cut admits. Name both images, a shared hook if any (shape, motion, sound), and the mix duration.
items.definition: A dissolve gradually overlaps the outgoing shot with the incoming shot so both images occupy the frame for a measurable duration. Opacity of A falls as opacity of B rises; at the midpoint you are looking at two ghosts.

items.name: Fade In / Fade Out
items.prompt: Fade to or from black around [Subject], chapter punctuation, sleep, death, or the start of a world. Name the field color if it is not black.
items.definition: A fade in or fade out takes the picture to or from a uniform field of black or color, rather than handing the frame straight to another visible scene. One side of the join is a world; the other side is absence, sleep, death, or a chapter break.

items.name: Wipe
items.prompt: Wipe replacing [Subject] with the next image, a line traveling across the frame, Star Wars grammar or a clock hand. Name direction, edge hardness, and both scenes.
items.definition: A wipe replaces one image with another through a moving boundary that travels across the frame. One side of the join is still A; the other side is already B; the edge between them is the edit, and it is meant to be seen.

items.name: Iris
items.prompt: Iris in or out on [Subject], a circular mask closing on a face or detail, silent-era pointing, or a wink. Name the center (an eye, a ring, a cat), whether the mask follows, and whether it opens or closes.
items.definition: An iris transition reveals or conceals the picture with a moving circular or shaped mask. The mask's center is a pointer: one side of the join is the full world, the other is a hole closing on a face, a detail, or black.

items.name: Cross-Cutting
items.prompt: Cross-cutting between [Subject] and a simultaneous other line, suspense by alternation, two clocks racing. Name both geographies, what the viewer is invited to assume, and whether that assumption is true.
items.definition: Cross-cutting alternates two or more locations or action lines, often implying they are happening at the same time. Each side of the join is a complete strand; the engine is meanwhile, two clocks racing.

items.name: Split Screen
items.prompt: Split screen with [Subject] in one pane and another life in the other, simultaneous spaces, phone-call cinema or dual identity. Name the boundary, whether eyelines match, and what each pane contains.
items.definition: Split screen shows two or more image fields at once, so separate spaces share a single moment on the same frame. Both sides of the join are visible together; there is no waiting for the next cut.

items.name: Montage
items.prompt: Montage sequence built around [Subject], time collapsed by images, training, travel, or a life in twenty shots. List the ordered images, what the collision claims, and whether time or idea is the engine.
items.definition: Film montage creates meaning or compression through the ordered juxtaposition of shots. Each side of a join is a complete image; the claim lives in the order, the collision, or the months squeezed into a minute.

items.name: Axial Cut
items.prompt: Axial cut jumping toward or away from [Subject] along the lens axis, punch-in without a zoom, a snap of scale. Name two or three matched framings, same angle, same pose, hard cuts.
items.definition: An axial cut jumps closer or farther along approximately the same camera axis, changing shot size without changing angle. The outgoing frame and the incoming frame share a viewpoint; only distance snaps.

items.name: Invisible Cut
items.prompt: Invisible cut hidden in [Subject]'s whip, a dark wall, or a passing body, the oner illusion. Name the hiding action, the before plate, the after plate, and that the camera path should appear continuous.
items.definition: An invisible cut hides an edit through motion, darkness, occlusion, blur, matching geometry, or digital stitching. One side of the join and the other are meant to feel like a single take; the splice is a seam the audience should not find.

items.name: J-Cut / L-Cut (Visual Setup)
items.prompt: A frame of [Subject] designed as the picture half of an L-cut or J-cut, reaction holding while another space is already speaking. For stills, describe a listening face or a doorway that can hold offscreen voice.
items.definition: A J-cut or L-cut visual setup is a picture designed so sound can lead or lag across the splice. One side of the join is a face, a room, or a listener that can hold; the other side is a space already speaking, or still speaking after we have left it.

items.name: Crash Cut
items.prompt: Crash cut on [Subject], two images colliding with no polite blend, a hard join that should sting. Name A and B, the scale or sound collision, and that B may already be mid-event.
items.definition: A crash cut slams two images together with no blend, so the join itself stings. One side of the splice and the other collide; unlike a smash that breaks an earned quiet, a crash cut often starts inside the event or hits like a drum from the first frame.

items.name: Flash Cut
items.prompt: Flash cut through [Subject], a few frames of another image interrupting, lightning in the edit. Name the present scene, the insert (and its duration in frames), and the return.
items.definition: A flash cut interrupts the present image with a few frames of another picture, then returns or races on before the insert can be studied. One side of the join is the ongoing scene; the other is lightning: a thought, a future, a wound, lasting a blink.

items.name: Match Motion
items.prompt: Match-motion cut on [Subject], direction and speed continuing across the join so the cut rides the movement. Name the outgoing path, the incoming path, matched pose and velocity, and what world changes.
items.definition: A match-motion cut continues direction and speed across the splice so the cut rides a vector even when location, time, or reality changes. One side of the join starts a movement; the other side keeps that movement, and the world around the body may be new.

items.name: Match Split
items.prompt: Match split of [Subject], a graphic divide that continues a line or motion into another space. Name the shared contour (horizon, table, eyeline), what each half contains, and that both are simultaneous.
items.definition: A match split continues a graphic line or motion across a divide, so one contour belongs to two worlds at once. One side of the join is a pane or half-frame; the other is its partner; the shared edge, horizon, or gesture is the match.

items.name: Quick Cuts
items.prompt: Quick cuts around [Subject], shots shorter than a breath, rhythm as violence or music. List a progression of sizes (wide to eyes, or hands to kit) and a duration curve.
items.definition: Quick cuts editing strings shots shorter than a breath, so duration itself becomes rhythm, pressure, or music. Each side of a join is a full view from a changing setup; the meaning is the rate, not a skip inside one frame.

items.name: Set Transition
items.prompt: Set transition around [Subject], the location transforming in camera, walls walking, one space becoming another. Name the starting architecture, the ending architecture, and that the camera does not hard-cut.
items.definition: A set transition lets the location change in camera: walls walk, architecture rewrites, one space becomes another without a hard cut. Both sides of the join are geographies that share a continuous camera path; the set itself is the editor.

items.name: Transitions
items.prompt: A designed transition around [Subject], the join as a gesture: wipe, morph, match, or light. Name both sides and the species of join.
items.definition: Film transitions are designed joins: the splice treated as a visible gesture rather than as continuity glue. One side of the join and the other are planned as a pair, and the audience is meant to notice how we left A and entered B.

items.name: Fragments
items.prompt: Fragments of [Subject], shattered coverage, pieces of a moment, the scene as shards. List the shards in causal order and name the missing master.
items.definition: Fragments, or fragmented editing, build an event from partial views, so the audience infers an action more complete than anything shown in one shot. Each side of a join is a shard: a blade, a mouth, a drain, a hand too late; the whole lives in the gaps.

items.name: Rain
items.prompt: Heavy rain around [Subject], backlit drops, wet-down pavement, umbrellas, silver streaks, weather as percussion. Name the backlight (a streetlamp, a sign, a HMI behind the rain), the wet ground, and drop size.
items.definition: Rain in film is falling water that makes air visible as streaks and turns the ground into a mirror. Drops are matter in the optical path; without backlight they vanish, and without a wet-down the street stays dry under a fake storm.

items.name: Fog
items.prompt: Dense fog around [Subject], depth collapsing, lamps becoming globes, figures appearing late. Name density (visibility in meters), the practicals blooming, and what is hidden.
items.definition: Fog is a dense local suspension of water droplets that collapses depth, turns lamps into globes, and delays the reveal of figures. The air is matter close to camera; geography hides until someone walks into the last few meters.

items.name: Mist
items.prompt: Light mist around [Subject], softer than fog, morning or mountain breath, layers of pale air. Name near-subject readability, paler far planes, and a backlight or low sun.
items.definition: Mist is a thinner water suspension than fog: pale layered air that still lets you read the next plane. Droplets are matter, but the veil is lyric, a morning or mountain breath rather than a wall.

items.name: Atmospheric Haze
items.prompt: Atmospheric haze stacking distance around [Subject], aerial perspective, far planes paler, depth as weather. Keep the near subject contrasty; name two or three receding planes.
items.definition: Atmospheric haze is scattering over distance: far planes go paler and often cooler, so kilometers of air become the depth cue. The particles are too small to read as drops; the air is matter you measure in ridges, not in globes around a near lamp.

items.name: Smoke
items.prompt: Smoke around [Subject], cigarette, chimney, or battle, shafts of light catching it, volume in the room. Name the source, the backlight or side key, and the direction of the ribbon.
items.definition: Smoke is combustion particles with a source, a direction, and enough density to turn a room's air into a volume the light can strike. Unlike weather fog, it has a chimney, a cigarette, a tire, or a battlefield; backlight carves it into shafts and swirls.

items.name: Dust Motes
items.prompt: Dust motes hanging in a shaft of light around [Subject], slow particles, a room that has been closed, time made visible. Name the window or slat, the dark surround, and that particles are discrete, not a fog fill.
items.definition: Dust motes are discrete particles hanging in a shaft of light, slow enough to read as time in still air. They are matter you can almost count; they live in the beam, not as a veil across the whole room.

items.name: Steam
items.prompt: Steam billowing around [Subject], trains, manholes, showers, a white veil, industrial or intimate heat. Name the hot source, the cold air, backlight, and rise.
items.definition: Steam is water vapor released where heat meets colder air: trains, manholes, showers, a white veil that rises and thins. It is wet matter, not combustion; it billows, condenses on lens and wool, and has a thermal source.

items.name: Snow
items.prompt: Falling snow around [Subject], large flakes in backlight, muffled world, tracks, winter silence you can see. Name flake size, a lamp or sun behind them, accumulation on shoulders and ground, and tracks if anyone has walked.
items.definition: Snow is ice falling and settling: large flakes in backlight, a muffled world, tracks that record who passed. The air holds crystals you can size; the ground accumulates; contrast goes soft because the world has been covered.

items.name: Wet-Down
items.prompt: Wet-down streets around [Subject], pavement sprayed for night, double the lights by reflection. Name the practicals, the sheeting water on asphalt, and empty air unless rain is also requested.
items.definition: A wet-down sprays pavement, asphalt, and cars so night lights double themselves in reflection, often with no rain in the air. The street is the effect; water is a surface treatment, not weather.

items.name: Sparks and Embers
items.prompt: Sparks or embers around [Subject], welding, fire, cigarettes, orange particles as weather. Name the source, color (white-orange to dull red), trajectory (fountain versus lofted drift), and a dark surround.
items.definition: Sparks and embers are incandescent particles thrown by welding, fire, grinding, or a cigarette: orange weather with short trajectories. They are burning matter; backlight is optional because they are their own small keys.

items.name: Dust and Sand
items.prompt: Dust or sandstorm wrapping [Subject], sun as a dull coin, silhouettes, grit in the highlights. Name wind direction, reduced visibility, and dirty speculars on skin and metal.
items.definition: Dust and sand as weather is mineral grit driven by wind until the sun is a dull coin and figures become silhouettes. The land attacks: particles occupy near air, sting highlights, and erase the horizon that haze would only pale.

items.name: Underwater
items.prompt: Underwater of [Subject], caustics, muffled space, hair and cloth in slow water, a world without horizon. Name depth, the surface as ceiling or absence, floating wardrobe, silt or bubbles in backlight.
items.definition: Underwater cinematography leaves air: the camera is in water, so caustics, buoyancy, and a missing horizon rewrite every edge. The medium is the matter; particles are silt and bubbles, and bodies move as if the world had gone slow without a slow-motion shutter.

items.name: Ocean
items.prompt: Ocean world of [Subject], swell, horizon, salt light, a person against water that does not care. Name sea state, scale (small figure or small boat), backlight on spray, and a hard horizon.
items.definition: Ocean cinematography treats the sea as the other actor: swell, a horizon, salt light, a person against water that does not care. The atmosphere is spray, haze over distance, and a moving floor; the camera is in air, on a hull, or on rocks, not yet in the lung of the sea.

items.name: Film Noir
items.prompt: Lead with the treatment, then lock physics. Film-noir treatment of [Subject], hard venetian gobos, unfilled far cheek, wet-down street bounce, 50mm spherical, 1940s crime blocking.
items.definition: Film noir lighting is a low-key, high-contrast setup: a hard key, often cut by a venetian gobo or a streetlamp cookie, leaves one cheek in true black while wet pavement returns silver. The camera sits at eye height on a 35mm or 50mm spherical lens, tungsten practicals as motivated sources, and blocking that isolates a figure in a doorway, an alley, or a pool of light.

items.name: Neo-Noir
items.prompt: Neo-noir look on [Subject], color where classic noir was silver, neon practicals, rain, contemporary crime blocking, hard key, unfilled far cheek. Name the hue of the signage and whether the camera is locked or tracking.
items.definition: Neo-noir cinematography keeps noir's hard keys and isolated blocking but replaces silver night with color: sodium vapor, neon practicals, and tungsten that stain rain and skin. The camera still hunts faces in shadow, yet the palette is contemporary, often cyan signage against warm flesh, not black-and-white contrast alone.

items.name: German Expressionism
items.prompt: German expressionist treatment of [Subject], painted shadows, impossible architecture, jagged hard light, dutch horizon, theatrical blocking. Name which wall or stair is illegally angled.
items.definition: German Expressionism cinematography treats the set as a mind: forced-perspective corridors, painted shadows, and jagged hard light replace natural architecture. The camera is often locked and slightly dutch, so the actor walks a geometry that already looks illegal.

items.name: Giallo
items.prompt: Giallo look on [Subject], hyper-saturated primaries, gelled window key, black leather implied in the foreground, 35mm zoom threat, Argento color crime. Name the red, green, or cobalt source.
items.definition: Giallo cinematography is Italian thriller grammar: hyper-saturated primaries from gelled windows and glass, fashion interiors, and a camera that often zooms rather than dollies toward threat. Beauty lighting sits on the victim. The violence is styled, not silver.

items.name: Spaghetti Western
items.prompt: 35, dusty ochre, hard noon sun, no fill, extreme close-up of eyes cut against a 24mm ridge. Name the dust and the holster height.
items.definition: Spaghetti western cinematography restages western iconography on Techniscope 2.35: dusty ochre landscapes, hard sun as the only key, and cuts from a 24mm plaza wide to a telephoto extreme close-up of eyes. Moral ambiguity sits in the hold on a face before anyone draws.

items.name: Found Footage
items.prompt: Found-footage camera on [Subject], consumer digital or Hi8, timestamp, autofocus hunt, amateur framing, operator-height, documentary panic. Name who holds the camera and why it stays on.
items.definition: The found footage look presents images as a recording made by someone inside the events, often later discovered or assembled, so the camera is a story object with a timestamp, a battery, and a reason to keep rolling. Consumer digital, Hi8, or MiniDV optics, autofocus hunt, and amateur framing are constraints, not decoration.

items.name: Cinéma Vérité
items.prompt: Cinéma vérité treatment of [Subject], available light, unpretty frames, zooming to find, mixed color temperature, life unstaged. Name the window or practical.
items.definition: Cinéma vérité uses available light, zoom-to-find framing, and the filmmaker's presence as a catalyst, so the camera is admitted into the room rather than hidden. Unpretty 16mm or digital frames, mixed color temperature, and a zoom hunting the moment are the physical signature, not a recovered amateur tape.

items.name: French New Wave
items.prompt: French New Wave energy on [Subject], location street light, handheld 35mm, jump cuts implied, jump-into-life framing, mixed cafe practicals. Name the sidewalk or apartment.
items.definition: French New Wave cinematography shoots fiction on locations with street light, handheld 16mm or 35mm, and an edit that will jump-cut rather than cover. The frame jumps into walking life: cafes, sidewalks, apartments with mixed practicals, and a camera that admits it is a camera.

items.name: Wuxia
items.prompt: Wuxia look on [Subject], misted bamboo or silk banners, wire-fu weightlessness implied, long-shot landscape, designed costume color, crane or wide hold. Name the weather and the path through air.
items.definition: Wuxia cinematography stages martial chivalry in landscape: misted bamboo or desert silk, long-shot geography, and wire-assisted paths that read as weightless rather than as street punching. Color is costume and fog, not a gelled murder window.

items.name: Tech Noir
items.prompt: Tech-noir on [Subject], future crime, screens as practicals, rain, corporate night, hard unfilled key, analog noir in a digital city. Name the display that lights the face.
